**Luke 1**
*Forasmuch as many have taken in hand to set forth in order a declaration of those things which are most surely believed among us,*

*2 Even as they delivered them unto us, which from the beginning were eyewitnesses, and ministers of the word;*

*3 It seemed good to me also, having had perfect understanding of all things from the very first, to write unto thee in order, most excellent Theophilus,*

*4 That thou mightest know the certainty of those things, wherein thou hast been instructed.*

*5 There was in the days of Herod, the king of Judaea, a certain priest named Zacharias, of the course of Abia: and his wife was of the daughters of Aaron, and her name was Elisabeth.*

*6 And they were both righteous before God, walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blameless.*

*7 And they had no child, because that Elisabeth was barren, and they both were now well stricken in years.*

*8 And it came to pass, that while he executed the priest's office before God in the order of his course,*

*9 According to the custom of the priest's office, his lot was to burn incense when he went into the temple of the Lord.*

*10 And the whole multitude of the people were praying without at the time of incense.*

*11 And there appeared unto him an angel of the Lord standing on the right side of the altar of incense.*

*12 And when Zacharias saw him, he was troubled, and fear fell upon him.*

*13 But the angel said unto him, Fear not, Zacharias: for thy prayer is heard; and thy wife Elisabeth shall bear thee a son, and thou shalt call his name John.*

*14 And thou shalt have joy and gladness; and many shall rejoice at his birth.*

*15 For he shall be great in the sight of the Lord, and shall drink neither wine nor strong drink; and he shall be filled with the Holy Ghost, even from his mother's womb.*

*16 And many of the children of Israel shall he turn to the Lord their God.*

*17 And he shall go before him in the spirit and power of Elias, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the disobedient to the wisdom of the just; to make ready a people prepared for the Lord.*

*18 And Zacharias said unto the angel, Whereby shall I know this? for I am an old man, and my wife well stricken in years.*

*19 And the angel answering said unto him, I am Gabriel, that stand in the presence of God; and am sent to speak unto thee, and to shew thee these glad tidings.*

*20 And, behold, thou shalt be dumb, and not able to speak, until the day that these things shall be performed, because thou believest not my words, which shall be fulfilled in their season.*

*21 And the people waited for Zacharias, and marvelled that he tarried so long in the temple.*

*22 And when he came out, he could not speak unto them: and they perceived that he had seen a vision in the temple: for he beckoned unto them, and remained speechless.*

*23 And it came to pass, that, as soon as the days of his ministration were accomplished, he departed to his own house.*

*24 And after those days his wife Elisabeth conceived, and hid herself five months, saying,*

*25 Thus hath the Lord dealt with me in the days wherein he looked on me, to take away my reproach among men.*

*26 And in the sixth month the angel Gabriel was sent from God unto a city of Galilee, named Nazareth,*

*27 To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin's name was Mary.*

*28 And the angel came in unto her, and said, Hail, thou that art highly favoured, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women.*

*29 And when she saw him, she was troubled at his saying, and cast in her mind what manner of salutation this should be.*

*30 And the angel said unto her, Fear not, Mary: for thou hast found favour with God.*

*31 And, behold, thou shalt conceive in thy womb, and bring forth a son, and shalt call his name* Jesus*.*

*32 He shall be great, and shall be called the Son of the Highest: and the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David:*

*33 And he shall reign over the house of Jacob for ever; and of his kingdom there shall be no end.*

*34 Then said Mary unto the angel, How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?*

*35 And the angel answered and said unto her, The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God.*

*36 And, behold, thy cousin Elisabeth, she hath also conceived a son in her old age: and this is the sixth month with her, who was called barren.*

*37 For with God nothing shall be impossible.*

*38 And Mary said, Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word. And the angel departed from her.*

*39 And Mary arose in those days, and went into the hill country with haste, into a city of Juda;*

*40 And entered into the house of Zacharias, and saluted Elisabeth.*

*41 And it came to pass, that, when Elisabeth heard the salutation of Mary, the babe leaped in her womb; and Elisabeth was filled with the Holy Ghost:*

*42 And she spake out with a loud voice, and said, Blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb.*

*43 And whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?*

*44 For, lo, as soon as the voice of thy salutation sounded in mine ears, the babe leaped in my womb for joy.*

*45 And blessed is she that believed: for there shall be a performance of those things which were told her from the Lord.*

*46 And Mary said, My soul doth magnify the Lord,*

*47 And my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour.*

*48 For he hath regarded the low estate of his handmaiden: for, behold, from henceforth all generations shall call me blessed.*

*49 For he that is mighty hath done to me great things; and holy is his name.*

*50 And his mercy is on them that fear him from generation to generation.*

*51 He hath shewed strength with his arm; he hath scattered the proud in the imagination of their hearts.*

*52 He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree.*

*53 He hath filled the hungry with good things; and the rich he hath sent empty away.*

*54 He hath helped his servant Israel, in remembrance of his mercy;*

*55 As he spake to our fathers, to Abraham, and to his seed for ever.*

*56 And Mary abode with her about three months, and returned to her own house.*

*57 Now Elisabeth's full time came that she should be delivered; and she brought forth a son.*

*58 And her neighbours and her cousins heard how the Lord had shewed great mercy upon her; and they rejoiced with her.*

*59 And it came to pass, that on the eighth day they came to circumcise the child; and they called him Zacharias, after the name of his father.*

*60 And his mother answered and said, Not so; but he shall be called John.*

*61 And they said unto her, There is none of thy kindred that is called by this name.*

*62 And they made signs to his father, how he would have him called.*

*63 And he asked for a writing table, and wrote, saying, His name is John. And they marvelled all.*

*64 And his mouth was opened immediately, and his tongue loosed, and he spake, and praised God.*

*65 And fear came on all that dwelt round about them: and all these sayings were noised abroad throughout all the hill country of Judaea.*

*66 And all they that heard them laid them up in their hearts, saying, What manner of child shall this be! And the hand of the Lord was with him.*

*67 And his father Zacharias was filled with the Holy Ghost, and prophesied, saying,*

*68 Blessed be the Lord God of Israel; for he hath visited and redeemed his people,*

*69 And hath raised up an horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David;*

*70 As he spake by the mouth of his holy prophets, which have been since the world began:*

*71 That we should be saved from our enemies, and from the hand of all that hate us;*

*72 To perform the mercy promised to our fathers, and to remember his holy covenant;*

*73 The oath which he sware to our father Abraham,*

*74 That he would grant unto us, that we being delivered out of the hand of our enemies might serve him without fear,*

*75 In holiness and righteousness before him, all the days of our life.*

*76 And thou, child, shalt be called the prophet of the Highest: for thou shalt go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways;*

*77 To give knowledge of salvation unto his people by the remission of their sins,*

*78 Through the tender mercy of our God; whereby the dayspring from on high hath visited us,*

*79 To give light to them that sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace.*

*80 And the child grew, and waxed strong in spirit, and was in the deserts till the day of his shewing unto Israel.*

And so we begin the Gospel according to Luke, the physician who journeyed with the apostle Paul, and was companion to evangelists throughout the churches. This (and the book of Acts), written as letters to "Theophilus." The identity of whom is subject to debate, but the term means "friend of God," and may be a general salutation to the saved, given the context; a declaration of those things which are most surely believed among us...*That thou mightest know the certainty of those things, wherein thou hast been instructed.*

Luke begins his recitation of events, not with genealogies of Mary and Joseph as Mark or Matthew, or the divine origins of Christ as God the way John does, but tells us the tale of John the Baptist's miraculous birth to Zacharias and Elizabeth.

Here we see their lineage is of Levi and or Aaron, the tribe of the priests of the temple. Zacharias (Zachariah) of the order of Abijah, the course of Abia in the Greek. When David was king he divided up the sons of Levi into various orders or courses, that they be born into tasks within the temple.

The course of Abia was responsible for maintaining the altar of incense. It was at this task that Zacharias was visited by the angel of the Lord, Gabriel, who brought God's promise that their prayers for a child would be answered as they were barren and in their old age. That they shall have a son and name him John, who will be a prophet making way for the coming of the Lord, that *the children of Israel shall he turn to the Lord their God. And he shall go before him in the spirit and power of Elias, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the disobedient to the wisdom of the just; to make ready a people prepared for the Lord.*

John was given the ministry to bring the children of Israel to turn to God, to repent.

This is the meaning of repentance, to turn towards something. To turn the hearts of the fathers towards their children, to turn the disobedient towards the wisdom of the just. To make a people mete for repentance. To make them ready for Jesus Christ that they might believe. When John is in the wilderness calling the people to repent, this is what it means.

Zacharias expresses doubt, and is struck dumb by the angel for unbelief, until the time of this birth be fulfilled.

Elizabeth becomes pregnant with John, and glorifies God for His mercy that He take away her reproach among men. Her embarrassment at being without child. She hides her condition for 5 months.

At the 6th, Gabriel appears unto Mary. A lowly virgin living in Galilee, in the city of Nazareth, in an area outside of Judea, formerly of the northern kingdom. Samaria. And we are told she is betrothed to Joseph, a descendant of David.

*Hail, thou that art highly favoured, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women.*

He tells her that she will bear a son, and name him Jesus. That He will be the heir promised of David who will be called *the Son of the Highest* and *the Lord God.* That He will rule forever, in a kingdom without end.

Mary asks how can this be, seeing she knows not man.

*And the angel answered and said unto her, The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God.*

And to shore up her faith, Gabriel tells her of her cousin Elizabeth and her miraculous pregnancy. *For with God nothing shall be impossible.*

This is important to note. Mary, as well as Zacharias and Elizabeth, all are blessed by God. Full glory and honor is given Him by Whom all things are possible. Zacharias and Elizabeth, we are told, were righteous in their faith and perfect in their ways. Not without sin (doubting the angel of the Lord is a sin), but chosen to be blessed for their faith. So too was Mary.

She gives consent to God to be used by Him in this manner, saying she is His handmaid, a servant. She believes God's word and is blessed with His promise. Just as the patriarchs and prophets were. Not because she was "sinless" or righteous on her own, but because she had faith and it was counted on for righteousness.

We learn that Mary spent the remainder of Elizabeth's term with her, and departed. John is born and so named, as the angel instructed Zacharias.

When people who know them hear this, they question why. And when mute Zacharias writes in faith that his son's name is John, he is freed from the curse and able to speak again. And the Holy Ghost comes upon him, and he gives praise to God almighty, prophesying in His name;

*Blessed be the Lord God of Israel; for he hath visited and redeemed his people, And hath raised up an horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David; As he spake by the mouth of his holy prophets, which have been since the world began: That we should be saved from our enemies, and from the hand of all that hate us; To perform the mercy promised to our fathers, and to remember his holy covenant; The oath which he sware to our father Abraham, That he would grant unto us, that we being delivered out of the hand of our enemies might serve him without fear, In holiness and righteousness before him, all the days of our life. And thou, child, shalt be called the prophet of the Highest: for thou shalt go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways; To give knowledge of salvation unto his people by the remission of their sins, Through the tender mercy of our God; whereby the dayspring from on high hath visited us, To give light to them that sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace.*

This is the promise of the Lord given witness by all the prophets. Don't miss this. Zacharias is showing, in the Spirit, how all is being fulfilled. With the mercy of God is with them. That his son shall prepare His way. To give knowledge of salvation, by the remission of sins. A light. A guide. Showing the way of peace. Because in sin, man is at enmity with God. But in Christ, God is offering peace on earth, goodwill towards man.

This is what was promised Abraham. Moses. David. All the prophets, up to and including John. Jesus is come.

I would note that the gospel of Luke is the most thorough regarding the nativity of Jesus. It's what Linus quotes from in the Charlie Brown Christmas special. It's often what we think of and read from at Christmas time. And as Luke writes, this is a *declaration of those things which are most surely believed among us.*

And so we should notice what is absent. Those things which are not commonly believed among the first century Christians to whom this gospel is addressed.

There is no mention of the immaculate conception of Mary. There is no indication she was born without sin. While she exclaims in the Spirit that future generations shall call her blessed, it isn't because of a special quality of her's, but by the works of God to whom she's a servant. Mary does the will of God through faith, and in faith is blessed among women to be chosen to bear the incarnation of Christ Jesus. This is the grace that God bestows upon her for her faith. For her willingness to believe.

Just like the Old Testament saints, Mary believed and it was counted upon her for righteousness. She was saved by faith alone and chosen because of that faith.

The Bible says that without faith we cannot please God. Mary could not please God without faith. Zacharias and Elizabeth could not please God without faith. None of them could be righteous absent their belief that God has provided them remission of sins in his mercy. Given the gift of salvation from His grace.

Removing this concept from the gospel, those that worship Mary missed the entire point and so they cannot understand God's mercy and they cannot receive God's grace.

**1 Timothy 3:16**

*And without controversy great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifest in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, seen of angels, preached unto the Gentiles, believed on in the world, received up into glory.*

Christ is born. Peace and goodwill from God to men.

 Merry Christmas

**Luke 2**
*And it came to pass in those days, that there went out a decree from Caesar Augustus that all the world should be taxed.*

*2 (And this taxing was first made when Cyrenius was governor of Syria.)*

*3 And all went to be taxed, every one into his own city.*

*4 And Joseph also went up from Galilee, out of the city of Nazareth, into Judaea, unto the city of David, which is called Bethlehem; (because he was of the house and lineage of David:)*

*5 To be taxed with Mary his espoused wife, being great with child.*

*6 And so it was, that, while they were there, the days were accomplished that she should be delivered.*

*7 And she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn.*

*8 And there were in the same country shepherds abiding in the field, keeping watch over their flock by night.*

*9 And, lo, the angel of the Lord came upon them, and the glory of the Lord shone round about them: and they were sore afraid.*

*10 And the angel said unto them, Fear not: for, behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people.*

*11 For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour, which is Christ the Lord.*

*12 And this shall be a sign unto you; Ye shall find the babe wrapped in swaddling clothes, lying in a manger.*

*13 And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host praising God, and saying,*

*14 Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men.*

*15 And it came to pass, as the angels were gone away from them into heaven, the shepherds said one to another, Let us now go even unto Bethlehem, and see this thing which is come to pass, which the Lord hath made known unto us.*

*16 And they came with haste, and found Mary, and Joseph, and the babe lying in a manger.*

*17 And when they had seen it, they made known abroad the saying which was told them concerning this child.*

*18 And all they that heard it wondered at those things which were told them by the shepherds.*

*19 But Mary kept all these things, and pondered them in her heart.*

*20 And the shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for all the things that they had heard and seen, as it was told unto them.*

*21 And when eight days were accomplished for the circumcising of the child, his name was called Jesus, which was so named of the angel before he was conceived in the womb.*

*22 And when the days of her purification according to the law of Moses were accomplished, they brought him to Jerusalem, to present him to the Lord;*

*23 (As it is written in the law of the Lord, Every male that openeth the womb shall be called holy to the Lord;)*

*24 And to offer a sacrifice according to that which is said in the law of the Lord, A pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons.*

*25 And, behold, there was a man in Jerusalem, whose name was Simeon; and the same man was just and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel: and the Holy Ghost was upon him.*

*26 And it was revealed unto him by the Holy Ghost, that he should not see death, before he had seen the Lord's Christ.*

*27 And he came by the Spirit into the temple: and when the parents brought in the child Jesus, to do for him after the custom of the law,*

*28 Then took he him up in his arms, and blessed God, and said,*

*29 Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace, according to thy word:*

*30 For mine eyes have seen thy salvation,*

*31 Which thou hast prepared before the face of all people;*

*32 A light to lighten the Gentiles, and the glory of thy people Israel.*

*33 And Joseph and his mother marvelled at those things which were spoken of him.*

*34 And Simeon blessed them, and said unto Mary his mother, Behold, this child is set for the fall and rising again of many in Israel; and for a sign which shall be spoken against;*

*35 (Yea, a sword shall pierce through thy own soul also,) that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed.*

*36 And there was one Anna, a prophetess, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Aser: she was of a great age, and had lived with an husband seven years from her virginity;*

*37 And she was a widow of about fourscore and four years, which departed not from the temple, but served God with fastings and prayers night and day.*

*38 And she coming in that instant gave thanks likewise unto the Lord, and spake of him to all them that looked for redemption in Jerusalem.*

*39 And when they had performed all things according to the law of the Lord, they returned into Galilee, to their own city Nazareth.*

*40 And the child grew, and waxed strong in spirit, filled with wisdom: and the grace of God was upon him.*

*41 Now his parents went to Jerusalem every year at the feast of the passover.*

*42 And when he was twelve years old, they went up to Jerusalem after the custom of the feast.*

*43 And when they had fulfilled the days, as they returned, the child Jesus tarried behind in Jerusalem; and Joseph and his mother knew not of it.*

*44 But they, supposing him to have been in the company, went a day's journey; and they sought him among their kinsfolk and acquaintance.*

*45 And when they found him not, they turned back again to Jerusalem, seeking him.*

*46 And it came to pass, that after three days they found him in the temple, sitting in the midst of the doctors, both hearing them, and asking them questions.*

*47 And all that heard him were astonished at his understanding and answers.*

*48 And when they saw him, they were amazed: and his mother said unto him, Son, why hast thou thus dealt with us? behold, thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing.*

*49 And he said unto them, How is it that ye sought me? wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?*

*50 And they understood not the saying which he spake unto them.*

*51 And he went down with them, and came to Nazareth, and was subject unto them: but his mother kept all these sayings in her heart.*

*52 And Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and man.*

**Luke 2** brings us to familiar ground with the recounting of the nativity of Jesus. Every man in the modern world has heard the details of this story, even if they choose not to believe them.

How all the world was taxed by Caesar, and returning to the city of David, where Joseph's lineage came from, Mary gave birth, laying Jesus in a manger, because there was no room for them in the inn.

That shepherds keeping watch over their flocks witness the angels of the Lord heralding His arrival. That God was extending peace, goodwill towards man. Tidings of great joy, which shall be to all the people. (All the people, not some, not chosen, all)

*For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour, which is Christ the Lord*.

The shepherds gather to witness that which the angels told them, and they spread the word throughout the countryside. Early evangelists, and those they preached to wondered at what they were told.

And Mary pondered these things in her heart.

After eight days, as was fitting the old covenant still in effect until the day of His resurrection, they took Jesus to the temple to be circumcised and be presented to the Lord. A sacrifice made of two turtledoves.

Simeon, who we are told was just by his faith in the coming Christ had the Holy Ghost upon him, and he came by His prompting to see the child, being told that before his death he would witness the Lord's Christ. He blessed the child and glorifies God, saying

*For mine eyes have seen thy salvation,*
*Which thou hast prepared before the face of all people; A light to lighten the Gentiles, and the glory of thy people Israel.*

The promise of the expected Christ was the faith that saved those who came before Jesus incarnation. Just as faith in His perfect work saves now. Trusting God's word, His promises and covenants. It has always been the sole means of salvation.

And again, the promise is to all people.

And again, Mary wonders at these things as Simeon in the Spirit prophesies that Jesus will fall and rise, and that it will be as if a sword pierces her soul, as the spear pierces His side.

They encounter Anna, a prophetess who in her old age as a widow, works in the temple for God. In the instant she saw the baby, she gave thanks to God and went and told all those who in faith looking forward to the redemption that the Messiah was here.

*And the child grew, and waxed strong in spirit, filled with wisdom: and the grace of God was upon him.*

Jesus, being fully man and fully God, was born as we are. He grew as we do. He waxed in spirit and filled with wisdom, meaning He grew into these things.

When we see the story of a young Jesus who tarries behind in the temple after going with His family to celebrate the feast of Passover, it is often portrayed as Jesus instructing the scribes there. But the Bible tells us that Jesus was seeking knowledge and understanding from them.

Yes He was fully God, but in the flesh, He was tempted, tested, in all things as we are, being fully man as well.

He waxed in spirit. He filled in wisdom. He grew physically and in knowledge.

*And it came to pass, that after three days they found him in the temple, sitting in the midst of the doctors, both hearing them, and asking them questions. And all that heard him were astonished at his understanding and answers.*

He astonished them with His ability to understand, but He sought to gain wisdom and knowledge. He was about His Father's business.

Some believe he came out of the womb with the full knowledge of everything, and had the whole word of God memorized in His heart, being the author of it. But this story found only in Luke paints a picture of a child who had to grow into a man as we do. And while He was perfect in His ways and without sin, that didn't mean He didn't hunger, thirst or have to devote Himself to learn scripture, just as we do. Jesus' did the will of His Father as an example to us. And God calls upon us to hear His word, question the meaning, learn His statutes, and commit His word to our hearts. Things that take discipline and faith, of which Jesus was the ultimate example.

And again, Mary took these things and remembered them, trying to understand just what it meant, that Jesus was Christ.

*For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin.*

The implications of this are important to consider. That Jesus as man had to, at every step of His life, choose to do the will of the Father, putting that above His own will and the weaknesses of the flesh He resided in.

Jesus had to choose to be without sin, though He suffered in the flesh. He chose to learn the word of God as a man would. Devote His time and energy to pleasing His heavenly Father and honoring His earthly parents. Not letting discomfort, cold, hunger, thirst, frustrations, humiliation, or any other thing being Him to sin. Yes the grace of God was upon Him. But we who are saved have a similar grace, but still sin.

He grew, He waxed in the Spirit. He grew in knowledge and wisdom, one day at a time, choosing at every opportunity to do the will of Him Who sent Him, so that He could call us to do the same. In that grace. In that love. Amen.

**Acts 7**
*Then said the high priest, Are these things so?*

*2 And he said, Men, brethren, and fathers, hearken; The God of glory appeared unto our father Abraham, when he was in Mesopotamia, before he dwelt in Charran,*

*3 And said unto him, Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and come into the land which I shall shew thee.*

*4 Then came he out of the land of the Chaldaeans, and dwelt in Charran: and from thence, when his father was dead, he removed him into this land, wherein ye now dwell.*

*5 And he gave him none inheritance in it, no, not so much as to set his foot on: yet he promised that he would give it to him for a possession, and to his seed after him, when as yet he had no child.*

*6 And God spake on this wise, That his seed should sojourn in a strange land; and that they should bring them into bondage, and entreat them evil four hundred years.*

*7 And the nation to whom they shall be in bondage will I judge, said God: and after that shall they come forth, and serve me in this place.*

*8 And he gave him the covenant of circumcision: and so Abraham begat Isaac, and circumcised him the eighth day; and Isaac begat Jacob; and Jacob begat the twelve patriarchs.*

*9 And the patriarchs, moved with envy, sold Joseph into Egypt: but God was with him,*

*10 And delivered him out of all his afflictions, and gave him favour and wisdom in the sight of Pharaoh king of Egypt; and he made him governor over Egypt and all his house.*

*11 Now there came a dearth over all the land of Egypt and Chanaan, and great affliction: and our fathers found no sustenance.*

*12 But when Jacob heard that there was corn in Egypt, he sent out our fathers first.*

*13 And at the second time Joseph was made known to his brethren; and Joseph's kindred was made known unto Pharaoh.*

*14 Then sent Joseph, and called his father Jacob to him, and all his kindred, threescore and fifteen souls.*

*15 So Jacob went down into Egypt, and died, he, and our fathers,*

*16 And were carried over into Sychem, and laid in the sepulchre that Abraham bought for a sum of money of the sons of Emmor the father of Sychem.*

*17 But when the time of the promise drew nigh, which God had sworn to Abraham, the people grew and multiplied in Egypt,*

*18 Till another king arose, which knew not Joseph.*

*19 The same dealt subtilly with our kindred, and evil entreated our fathers, so that they cast out their young children, to the end they might not live.*

*20 In which time Moses was born, and was exceeding fair, and nourished up in his father's house three months:*

*21 And when he was cast out, Pharaoh's daughter took him up, and nourished him for her own son.*

*22 And Moses was learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and was mighty in words and in deeds.*

*23 And when he was full forty years old, it came into his heart to visit his brethren the children of Israel.*

*24 And seeing one of them suffer wrong, he defended him, and avenged him that was oppressed, and smote the Egyptian:*

*25 For he supposed his brethren would have understood how that God by his hand would deliver them: but they understood not.*

*26 And the next day he shewed himself unto them as they strove, and would have set them at one again, saying, Sirs, ye are brethren; why do ye wrong one to another?*

*27 But he that did his neighbour wrong thrust him away, saying, Who made thee a ruler and a judge over us?*

*28 Wilt thou kill me, as thou diddest the Egyptian yesterday?*

*29 Then fled Moses at this saying, and was a stranger in the land of Madian, where he begat two sons.*

*30 And when forty years were expired, there appeared to him in the wilderness of mount Sina an angel of the Lord in a flame of fire in a bush.*

*31 When Moses saw it, he wondered at the sight: and as he drew near to behold it, the voice of the Lord came unto him,*

*32 Saying, I am the God of thy fathers, the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. Then Moses trembled, and durst not behold.*

*33 Then said the Lord to him, Put off thy shoes from thy feet: for the place where thou standest is holy ground.*

*34 I have seen, I have seen the affliction of my people which is in Egypt, and I have heard their groaning, and am come down to deliver them. And now come, I will send thee into Egypt.*

*35 This Moses whom they refused, saying, Who made thee a ruler and a judge? the same did God send to be a ruler and a deliverer by the hand of the angel which appeared to him in the bush.*

Here in Luke chapter 3, we find his goal, stated in the opening of his Gospel to "*set forth in order a declaration of those things which are most surely believed among us*," being met, giving precise details to the time in which John the Baptist, followed by Jesus, began their ministry. Luke establishes who was in charge, and where, pinpointing for readers the time and place of this happening, with familiar figures of their recent past; *That thou mightest know the certainty of those things, wherein thou hast been instructed.*

And so we find John, born roughly 6 months ahead of Jesus, has fulfilled the prophecy given his father by Gabriel, to be the answer to the prophecy given Isaiah; the voice in the wilderness making straight the paths of the Lord.

In the times before modernity, when the lords and kings would travel abroad, often in caravans, taking weeks or months to get where they were going, a group of their servants would run ahead, both to herald their lord's passing to prepare those in the path chosen to receive their king, and to make certain the road was clear. That the way was smooth. Harbingers and workmen.

So too, Christ the Lord was coming and the paths were to be made straight for Him.

In scripture, we often see the idea of walking in God's statutes, following His wisdom, being righteous by obeying His sayings, is compared to walking a path. Turning neither to the left not right. But following the narrow way of the Lord.

John, the harbinger of the Lord is sent by God to spiritually make straight the paths, to bring the people to repentance, turning towards His Son. Baptizing those who believed, a picture of Christ's crucifixion, burial and resurrection, and a symbol of their being washed clean by the remission of sins. Preparing them that shall see the salvation of God among them. Exhorting those who were saved to now do the works meet for repentance. Charity. Proper living. Changed as those who are free from the wrath should live.

John is filled with the Holy Ghost, as promised, and speaks boldly and with authority the words of God. He is the first prophet of the Lord to have the Holy Ghost upon him in 400 years. His hard preaching against sin and of the word of God, scripture, draws people from all over the region.

We see the lands mentioned by ruler, and it encompasses all of Judea, up into Samaria and the provinces from the sea and in and around Jordan, and it is from these places that multitudes come to hear John preach and to be baptized.

In **Matthew 3** we see that this draws attention of the Pharisees and Sadducees, and that the preaching he does, also shown in **Luke 3**, is an indictment of the Jews, especially their religious leaders.

*O generation of vipers, who hath warned you to flee from the wrath to come? Bring forth therefore fruits meet for repentance: And think not to say within yourselves, We have Abraham to our father: for I say unto you, that God is able of these stones to raise up children unto Abraham.*

John speaking in the Spirit says that if they are truly there repentant of their false ways, show the fruit of it. Especially the religious leaders who have not the fruits, the souls prepared to repent towards God. They've failed the people. They have rested on the fact that they are God's "chosen." They haven't prepared anyone for the salvation to come.

This generation of vipers has believed that by the nature of their lineage they would be saved. This is the same mistaken idea behind dispensationalism and the "God's not done with the Jews!" mentality among so many misguided and judaized Christians today.

But John repudiates the idea of special treatment for the Jews. He says God could raise up Israelites from rocks if He so chose. They aren't special boys. And they certainly aren't living in a manner that shows God-fearing reverence for Him and His laws.

The people ask themselves if he is the Christ, and he responds that one greater than him comes, who he isn't fit to untie His shoes. That the savior to come will not baptize with water, but with the Holy Ghost, and with fire, burning the chaff and gathering the wheat.

And so, Jesus comes to be baptized, to do the will of His Father.

*And the Holy Ghost descended in a bodily shape like a dove upon him, and a voice came from heaven, which said, Thou art my beloved Son; in thee I am well pleased.*

Amen.

But John's preaching against sin, especially of the political and religious leaders of that day, leads him to conflict with Herod, who had taken his brother's wife, among other evils, and so John is locked up in prison.

It is at this time where Jesus, being around 30 years of age, begins His earthly ministry.

Luke, having established the time and circumstances surrounding these events, then gives his version of the generations of Jesus, going from his stepfather Joseph's lineage. Perfect in his generations, all the way back to Adam, who we are reminded, was begat of God.

Being the son of Joseph, even adopted, places Jesus in line for the throne of David, fulfilling the prophets sayings that there will be a King from the root of Jesse, a descendant of David, who would rule and reign forever. The Son of David.

To the more secular, this places Jesus in line to be an earthly king. To make the Christ the physical deliverer of Israel. But to those called by the Spirit, and given understanding of scripture, the savior of their souls and heir to the Heavenly Kingdom. The Son of God.

It is these two sonships that Jesus was born into. Fully God. Fully man. And the conflict in the hearts of those who hear of Him, even those who directly saw Him walk among them performing miracles and preaching on the Kingdom of God, would set the stage for His ministry.

**Luke 3:9-14**
*And now also the axe is laid unto the root of the trees: every tree therefore which bringeth not forth good fruit is hewn down, and cast into the fire. And the people asked him, saying, What shall we do then? He answereth and saith unto them, He that hath two coats, let him impart to him that hath none; and he that hath meat, let him do likewise.*

*Then came also publicans to be baptized, and said unto him, Master, what shall we do? And he said unto them, Exact no more than that which is appointed you. And the soldiers likewise demanded of him, saying, And what shall we do? And he said unto them, Do violence to no man, neither accuse any falsely; and be content with your wages.*

John the Baptist is in the wilderness, preaching to the masses of people from all around Judea and the surrounding countries, who have come to hear the word of God preached, under the power of the Holy Ghost.

Many repent and believe and are baptized in expectation of the Christ. But they, as babes, don't know what to do, now that they are saved. What does this mean in practice? How is it applied in their lives. John says that dead trees will be hewn down and burned. Like the vipers of the Pharisees and Sadducees who do not produce any fruit, they're not bringing people to turn towards God. They aren't doing works of charity. As Jesus will later preach, they are hypocrites and worse. But those who by hearing the word of God come to faith, not wanting to be as the vipers, the fruitless, pricked in their conscience by the word, not wanting to be hewn down, they ask "What shall we do?"

And to the publicans, who were tax collectors, a group known for their overcharging, abusing their office and taking bribes, he says take no more than you're appointed to, basically to be honest in your dealings. To the soldiers, he answers in a similar manner. He says not to commit violence, or falsely accuse or to covet more than his wages. Basically, don't abuse your position of power.

Of course, all of this can be boiled down to "Love thy neighbor," which many of us overlook because it is such a basic teaching. Even unbelieving unregenerate man know the golden rule. And they knew it then, too. It was part of the law. God commanded it of them in **Leviticus 19:18**

*Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the Lord.*

But what does that look like in practice? How do we as saved Christians, at liberty in Christ, having repented of our past beliefs and acknowledged we are sinners destined to Hell but for the grace of God and are now saved, what do we do now?

And John's answer to these people, 2000 years ago, remains the answer today. In your daily life, don't defraud people. Don't steal. Don't abuse whatever authority you have, at work or at home. Don't lie. Don't behave as the vipers, hypocrites and unbelievers. Love others the way you want to be loved. The way you trust in Christ to love you.

And so, at work, do you slack? Steal time from the boss? Take advantage of your position? Lie to others? Gossip? Covet the status of wealth of others? Commit adultery? Not even that adultery of the heart Jesus warned us of?

At home, do you love your spouse as Christ loves the church? Jealously and putting their well being before your own? Honoring your parents? Not coveting your neighbors possessions?

Are you a blessing to your community? To your church family? To strangers? Are you a light that shines, magnifying God's love for you that others may come to ask you why you're full of love and hope?

Luke chapter 4 picks up with Jesus after His baptism in the Jordan and by the Holy Spirit, having been proclaimed by the Father "His Son, in whom Im well pleased."

The Gospel says, Jesus was led of the Spirit to the wilderness, and there to fast and be tempted by Satan, 40 days. It is often overlooked that the three instances given here and in the other Gospels are not the only tests of the devil Jesus suffered. He was tempted 40 days.

Jesus hungered. He thirst. He was weary. He was alone. Without shelter. Cold at night. Hot in the sun of the day. In all ways tempted as we are. But without sin.

And Jesus was led of the Spirit to this temptation, He was not given a pass, was not brought to the temple in Jerusalem to preach the Gospel to an adoring throng of people. He was brought to desolate places where the prince of this world would tempt Him.

Satan, the accuser of the brethren, seeking to corrupt the Christ, and derail God's plan of salvation for the world, tested and tried Jesus that he may go before the Father and say, "your Son is not worthy to be a sacrifice. He is not without blemish." But Jesus withstood Satan, and in doing so, gave us the pattern for dealing with temptation in our lives.

The Bible says Jesus was tempted as we are. Knows our infirmities and understanding, shows mercy on us. We are not given more than we can handle. If we reject Satan, God will provide us a way.

That way is found in what Jesus used to resist Satan. The word of God.

So understanding that Jesus did not have some special means to supernaturally avoid succumbing to sin, it wasn't His divine nature that saved His human flesh from falling, but His doing His Father's will, and clinging to the word.

Jesus was hungry and weak, and the devil said to turn a stone to bread. A temptation of the flesh. To satisfy the immediate need to please ourselves physically.

And Jesus replied *It is written, That man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word of God.*

Note His use of "it is written." That man loves not by bread. Not by the needs of the flesh. That there is more to this than satisfying our physical desires but that we live by *every word of God*.

He quotes scripture to put of the devil from Him. Every word of God is all we need to live. (The presupposition is that, in order to be true, we have access to every word of God. Thus the preservation of His word). This having double meaning, as the manna in the desert was a picture of Christ, Jesus who is the bread of life come down from Heaven, and He is the Word of God made flesh, through whom eternal life is given to all who believe.

And Jesus, using God's word, rebukes Satan.

Then, tempting Jesus with power, Satan offers Him the thrones of this world, of whom Satan is god. Given power to influence kings and regents. The spirits that bring wickedness to high places. Overseeing the principalities of the rulers of the darkness of this world. By supernatural means, he takes Jesus to the top of a mountain and shows Him all the lands of man in the world. The devil says to Jesus, worship me and I will give you an earthly kingdom, ultimate power.

And Jesus, again citing scripture rejects him; *for it is written, Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve.* And again the power of the knowledge of God's word saves Jesus from temptation.

Finally, frustrated, Satan places Jesus upon the spire of the temple in Jerusalem. Hundreds of feet in the air. And says to jump, because the scriptures say that God the Father would not suffer to see even His foot dash against the rocks. That God would send angels to stop Jesus from even stubbing His toe, so surely they would catch Him.

*And Jesus answering said unto him, It is said, Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God.*

Again, using scripture, Jesus turns aside Satan and his temptations.

And the devil departs having failed to stand against the word of God. In Matthew we read; *Then the devil leaveth him, and, behold, angels came and ministered unto him.*

By faith of this Jesus endured, that God the Father would provide. That He loved Him and was true. Not slack in His promise. By turning to scripture, Jesus resisted sin, and was rewarded for His trust.

This is the pattern for our lives. The path we follow, led by Christ. When the Spirit leads us into the wilderness. When we are weak, and tired and hungry. When we are in peril, as Jesus upon the steeples of the Temple. When we are at our lowest physically and mentally, Satan will come to tempt us. And when he does, we can know that none of what he offers us to sin, none of the temporary satisfactions of the flesh, are beyond our means to resist as long as we turn to God, stay in His word, and have faith that our needs will be met by Him Who loves us.

It is our daily walk with God that protects us. We ask Him to provide our daily bread, not just physical need for food, but spiritually, studying the word of God. We start our day in prayer, taking to God, and reading His word that His will be made known to us. His promises made clear that we may grow in faith. This is how we resist temptation. This is how we keep Satan at bay.

We are weak in the flesh, but if we feed the spirit, the "new man," as Paul describes it, that quickened spirit that is the surety of our eternal life, we shall overcome as Jesus has overcome.

And when we walk after the flesh, and neglect our prayers and our reading of the word, and we get caught up in the cares of this world, the way Satan caught up Jesus to the top of that mountain, to the heights of the temple, and we fear, and lust, feel wrath, covet and put ourselves at risk tempting God, and have not the means to escape though God has given them to us. His word; The pattern made by Christ to follow.

It should be mentioned that before beginning His earthly ministry, Jesus sought to purify himself with prayer and fasting. Legitimate fasting, denying Himself not personal taste and treats, preference and privilege, but actually sacrificing physical necessity that He may focus on the things of God. The word. In prayer and supplication.

How can those who deny that we have "every word of God" and that don't read it daily, allowing other men to be an intermediary, how can they resist temptation? If their prayers are to other men, not boldly going before God the Father with supplication?

They can't.

That's why they often seek worldly power. It's why they fast and pray to be seen of men, and not locked away as God commands. Not going into the wilderness but proclaiming their "sacrifice" to the world. It's why they tempt God.

I will continue the rest of the chapter later. The chapters in Luke are long and cover multiple stories of Christ.

We will see later in this chapter that Jesus again quotes scripture to the people and we should note that already in the past 3 chapters, and all through the book, the scriptures are referenced constantly. The law and Psalms and words of the prophets.

Because, *All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness: That the man of God may be perfect, throughly furnished unto all good works.*

Man lives *by every word of God.*

Biblical fundamentalism. That God's word is the only and final authority. All we need for doctrine that we may be perfect, whole, complete.

It was good enough for Jesus in the desert against Satan. It is good enough for us today who follow Him.

Picking up where we left off in Luke 4 yesterday, we find Jesus at the start of His earthly ministry. Having just been baptized and anointed by the Spirit, and proclaimed by the Father as His Son, and having fasted, prayed and withstanding the devil in the wilderness for 40 days, the Bible says Jesus was full of the power of the Spirit, and returned to His home province of Galilee, where He taught in the synagogues of God, gaining fame and renown throughout the area.

We see that Jesus ministry begins in the remnant of the Northern Kingdom of Israel, outside of Judea, but preaching to the lost sheep of Israel. In these times, synagogues were the local churches of those who worshipped God. Where they would go, not only weekly on the Sabbath but throughout the week, to hear God's word read from scriptures, to pray and to learn about God's word. The Temple in Jerusalem was for feasts and sacrifices and pilgrims, but the communities abroad had independent, fundamentalist gatherings, or churches that people attended.

**Psalms 74:8**
*They said in their hearts, Let us destroy them together: they have burned up all the synagogues of God in the land.*

Note the Bible says there was a time synagogues were of God. It wasn't until after Christ where the unrepentant Jews were made a synagogue of Satan by the Lord, rejected. Reprobate.

And Luke tells us that going to these houses of worship was Jesus' custom. It was His routine. Oh to be like Jesus and make going to church to read, hear and learn the word of God as part of our custom. To be our routine.

And of course, just as churches are today, the synagogues were likely hit or miss in regards to what they taught, how they acted, if they produced fruit meet for repentance, if they were ice cold or lukewarm or red hot for the Lord. I am sure Jesus Christ Himself sat through boring sermons, by dull preachers who were wrong on doctrine, in congregations of people who were sinners and hypocrites or holier than thous. But it was Jesus' custom. And so, to begin His work, Jesus went to church. We should too.

Now having established somewhat of a following throughout Galilee, Jesus returns to Nazareth, the town He grew up in. Where He lived as a child with Mary and Joseph, His half brothers and sisters. Where He developed the habit of going to synagogue. He returns full of the Spirit, and is called to read, and He preaches the prophecy of Christ from **Isaiah 61:1-2**
*The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me; because the Lord hath anointed me to preach good tidings unto the meek; he hath sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to them that are bound; To proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord, and the day of vengeance of our God; to comfort all that mourn;*

Note He leaves off the day of vengeance. That is His second coming. Here He is at His first.

**John 3:17**
*For God sent not his Son into the world to condemn the world; but that the world through him might be saved.*

And so, Jesus reads this scripture foretelling His coming, and says, with every eye on Him; *This day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears*.

For those who doubt that Jesus ever proclaimed Himself to be the Christ, here He is saying precisely that. From the beginning. In no uncertain terms.

And the crowd becomes incredulous. "Is this not the Son of Joseph?" They knew Him, watched Him grow, saw Him in synagogue.

In response we are given the first record of Jesus preaching in Luke;

*Ye will surely say unto me this proverb, Physician, heal thyself: whatsoever we have heard done in Capernaum, do also here in thy country. And he said, Verily I say unto you, No prophet is accepted in his own country.*

In **Mark 6**, we get more detail of this part; *A prophet is not without honour, but in his own country, and among his own kin, and in his own house.*

Basically, those who know us best, whose familiarity has them over comfortable in their understanding. Many Christians can relate to this, where after being born again we try to share the good news with relatives or friends, and they, knowing us intimately, scoff. "You? I saw you that one time..." Or even just see us as the child they watched grow and can't accept that you've got something to offer them in your youth. It's why it can be difficult for a Christian to get members of his own family saved.

And so, being rejected of His hometown crowd, Jesus doubles down and preaches even harder, using scripture. He says, citing **1 Kings 17**, you remember Elijah, how he was rejected and shut up the heavens that it didn't rain for 3 and a half years? That in Israel was great famine? The Spirit led the prophet to a Gentile widow in the land of Zidon who, along with her son was about to die of hunger, having only one meager meal left between them. God sent Elijah there because of her faith. In the story she offers the food to the prophet in faith, even though it was all she had. And God works a miracle where they are all fed and sustained with what little she had until the time of famine was over.

Jesus says, I bet there were many widows starving in Israel. But it was a Gentile woman who He saved.

Then, Jesus mentions **2 Kings** 5, and the prophet Elisha, where a Syrian, the captain of the hosts of the army of the king, suffered leprosy. Jesus says that many lepers were in Israel in the time, but it was this Gentile that God sent His prophet to heal.

That the prophets were rejected of their own, and so the healing power of God, His blessings and promises went to others. To Gentiles.

**John 1:11**
*He came unto his own, and his own received him not.*

Jesus spitting fire, using scripture, He rebukes and reproaches His countrymen for their rejection of the word of God, the Gospel of truth He's brought to them, in a prefigure of the rejection He would face of the Jews at large, and prophesying God's turn to the Gentiles that would receive Him. And in a like manner, the crowd engaged at their own sin being pointed out, gathered to kill Jesus. They bring Him to the top of a hill, looking to cast Him off headlong.
But Jesus, as He will do throughout His ministry after crowds of Jews offended by His hard preaching turn on Him, supernaturally passed by out of the crowd. His time having not yet come.

Afterwards, we are told, Jesus *came down to Capernaum, a city of Galilee, and taught them on the sabbath days. And they were astonished at his doctrine: for his word was with power.*

It was more fruitful here. And while He could not perform miracles in Nazareth by their lack of faith, here Jesus begins to heal multitudes.

Luke being a physician focuses often on the healing power of Christ during his Gospel.

A man possessed by an unclean devil is exercised, the demon recognizing Jesus as the Christ. *Let us alone; what have we to do with thee, thou Jesus of Nazareth? art thou come to destroy us? I know thee who thou art; the Holy One of God.*

And the people are amazed; *with authority and power he commandeth the unclean spirits, and they come out.*

Luke tells us that Jesus heals Simon's mother, rebuking the fever she had, and being healed, she set about serving them food.

Because of these miracles, a multitude brought their sick or possessed loved ones to be healed. *And devils also came out of many, crying out, and saying, Thou art Christ the Son of God. And he rebuking them suffered them not to speak: for they knew that he was Christ.* His time not yet come, and relying on the people to repent by faith, seen by the signs and hearing of the word, Jesus repeatedly tells the unclean spirits to be silent about who He is.

And even when Jesus had left the city for the wilderness, to travel to other places with the word, the people followed Him. He gently reproaches them that He must go to others too. And so, His ministry grows throughout the land of Galilee.

Now, one last thing. I wrote about this last night and want to reemphasize the point.

The first public preaching of Jesus we are given in Luke is Jesus reading Isaiah's prophecy of His (first and second) coming;

*The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised, To preach the acceptable year of the Lord.*

As I point out in the linked post, this serves as a mission statement, the founding and guiding principle of Jesus ministry on earth. The same ministry we who are saved are called to continue, until He returns.

Really ruminate on this verse. It is what we are appointed to do if we are following Christ. The application of this concept can change our lives as Christians. Don't miss it.

So we are there in Luke chapter 5, and we find Jesus ministry in Galilee is thriving. Multitudes are coming out to hear His preaching and to be healed of infirmities, cleansed of evil spirits and many who end up getting saved.

One such is Simon, who we are told in the Gospel of John Jesus dubs Peter, or stone. Peter's brother Andrew, a follower of John the Baptist, tells his sibling "We have found the Messias," the Christ. The sons of Jonah were faithful to the coming of Christ. Peter was meet for repentance.

It's in this context we see Jesus used Simon to enable Him to preach to the throng pressing Jesus up to the waters edge along the shore, by using his fishing boat which Peter, still Simon at this point, willingly allows Him to do. In recompense, Jesus performs a miracle, filling their nets to overflowing with fish after a night of fishing with no bites.

*When Simon Peter saw it, he fell down at Jesus' knees, saying, Depart from me; for I am a sinful man, O Lord.*

It is in this manner we all come before Jesus for salvation. Calling upon the name of the Lord, in acknowledgement we are sinners and not worthy of Him.

And Jesus tells Peter, Andrew, and the sons of Zebedee, James and John to follow Him, and become fishers of men. Just as we who seek to follow Jesus are called to do.

Next Luke gives us an example of the healing that is a theme of his gospel, being a physician, in this the healing of a leaper who shows great faith and humility "*Lord, if thou wilt, thou canst make me clean."* Again, a picture of the manner in which we are saved. Calling upon the mercy of the Lord to make us clean, with the faith to know He is able to.

Jesus heals him, and cautions him to keep the manner of it to himself, but to go to the temple and offer the sacrifice for cleansing from leprosy given of Moses, found in **Leviticus 14**.

It is a complicated ritual, one that must have seen little use in the times it was given in the law, as leprosy is untreatable and the healing from it coming only from a miracle. Yet Moses in the Spirit gives the process in the law, with specificity. I quoted only the first part of the ceremonial sacrifices, but it takes up basically an entire chapter. But nothing in the Bible is accidental, coincidental or incidental.

First the leper goes to the priests who will send one out of the camp, out to the wilderness, to check the man and confirm they are healed. A testimony given, as Jesus says here.

Then the priest must take two birds alive and clean, and cedar wood, and scarlet, and hyssop, and place one of the birds in an earthen vessel, and kill it, sprinkling the blood of the dead bird on the living bird, the wood, the scarlet cloth and the hyssop, and then sprinkle the blood from these items and the living bird on the healed man, 7 times, proclaiming him clean, and releasing the second bird to the wild.

The bird in the earthen vessel, the clay that man is made from, as a substitutionary sacrifice, its blood upon wood, like the wood of the cross. On the scarlet, as the garments of Christ were so stained. On the hyssop, like the sprig dipped in vinegar, given to Jesus on the cross. And this blood of atonement then cleanses the man, and the living bird, like the risen Christ ascends to the heavens.

The other sacrifices require lambs without blemish, etc, and are equally pictures of Christ Jesus. It's a fascinating chapter to read and study on. Placed in the OT that a testimony of Jesus could be made when he healed this man.

We see a pattern in the Gospels, especially of Luke, where after successful outings in His ministry, Jesus would often go to the wilderness by Himself to pray and rest. This he does here and then, we pick up later He is gathering fame and multitudes are coming to see Him, especially that the sick may be healed.

And so, the crowd surrounds a house where Jesus is teaching and healing, and in the crowd came Pharisees and scribes, "doctors of the law," come to see Jesus.

A lame man, bedridden, is taken by 4 friends to be healed of Jesus, but they cannot find a way to get him through the crowd. But, so great is their faith that this miracle could be done, they devise a plan and climbing the building, lower their friend through the roof, down before Jesus.

And Jesus, amazed at the faith and loyalty of him and his friends, says to the man "*thy sins are forgiven thee.*"

Not that he was healed physically, but by faith brought to forgiveness. Just as we are often brought to Jesus by our friends. Carried to this justification in faith by the faith of others. Just as we are to carry our own friends to the presence of the Lord. What love that is!

And the Pharisees and lawyers wonder to themselves, "Who but God can forgive sin?"

And Jesus knowing their hearts, answers;

*What reason ye in your hearts? Whether it is easier, to say, Thy sins be forgiven thee; or to say, Rise up and walk? But that ye may know that the Son of man hath power upon earth to forgive sins, (he said unto the sick of the palsy,) I say unto thee, Arise, and take up thy couch, and go into thine house.*

And the man, healed, leaps up and carrying his cot, leaves rejoicing and praising God.

Everyone present is amazed. Many praise God for what they've witnessed. Some, filled with fear. Even the miracles and signs and wonders were not enough for them to believe. Only to say "*We have seen strange things to day*."

Returning to **Luke 5**, we pick up with Jesus calling a publican named Levi, who we know as Matthew, who we're told, *left all, rose up, and followed* Jesus.

Now publicans, who worked for the occupational governments of the Roman empire collecting duties and taxes, were looked down upon by the the people under their jurisdiction, who naturally resent their fellow countrymen serving the foreign state against them, and were often as corrupt and crooked as they still are today. Further, Matthew was of the tribe of Levi, who were called to be the priesthood under the Old Testament, and so must have been particularly a pariah in these times. But by faith he answers the call and leaves all to follow Christ.

And for him, as it is for us, his salvation is a cause for celebration. He has wealth and status among others in his profession, and calls those he knows together a feast, inviting Jesus and His disciples.

To this, as is often the case throughout the Gospels, the envious and bitter Jews, in this case the Pharisees, see the opportunity to criticize Jesus, asking why he is hanging out with sinners like Levi/Matthew. To which, Jesus replies "*They that are whole need not a physician; but they that are sick. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.*"

This is the purpose of Christ's ministry and our commission to give the Gospel to the poor. To the heartbroken. To those in bondage to sin. To set them at liberty with the good news of salvation. Just as Jesus stated in His reading of **Isaiah 61** that we just covered; It is the mission statement of the Lord.

Also detect a hint of rebuke, in that Jesus mentions the righteous in this saying somewhat sarcastically to give a ribbing to the self-righteous Pharisees. They, of course respond with another accusation, questioning why Jesus' disciples don't routinely fast as they do. (They lump John the Baptist's followers in there to lend themselves some of his credibility.)

But, Jesus knows their hearts, that they are vipers. Hypocrites. As He tells in a parable later on in **Luke 18** that seems based on exactly this encounter:

*Two men went up into the temple to pray; the one a Pharisee, and the other a publican.*

*The Pharisee stood and prayed thus with himself, God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even as this publican. I fast twice in the week, I give tithes of all that I possess. And the publican, standing afar off, would not lift up so much as his eyes unto heaven, but smote upon his breast, saying, God be merciful to me a sinner. I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other: for every one that exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted.*

Note that the Pharisees took pride in their ritual fasting, as well as their tithing and temple attendance and all the rest. They saw themselves as righteous by their works and better than, holier than, the humble publican, a sinner who may not have done these rituals and rites but who understands his place and the undeserved mercy and grace of the Lord.

There are commandments of the Lord that we are given, things He tells us we must do. We must believe the Gospel. We must share it with others, for example. Then there are things we are expected to do, but not commanded as such. We are not told we must fast, but Jesus tells us how to when we do;

**Matthew 6:16-18**
*Moreover when ye fast, be not, as the hypocrites, of a sad countenance: for they disfigure their faces, that they may appear unto men to fast. Verily I say unto you, They have their reward.*

Notice He says "*when* you fast." It is assumed we will fast, at the appropriate time, called by the Spirit, when we have a need to align ourselves to God's will and build our faith. Fasting in the Bible wasn't a sign of righteousness or a way to get God to do our will, but usually done at a sign of trouble or turmoil in the person's life. A death in the family, a tough or perilous time. At the beginning of a trial.

Like Jesus in the wilderness before beginning His ministry. A way to align ourselves with the will of God that we may better understand and come to peace with it. That the Spirit may move in us and increase our faith as we deny our flesh.

Fasting isn't to earn brownie points with God, to get him to do our will. It most certainly isn't done in an outward sign to earn the approval of men.

Understanding this, and that the Pharisees had the wrong idea about what fasting's purpose is, and how righteousness is achieved, Jesus replies to their accusation;

*Can ye make the children of the bridechamber fast, while the bridegroom is with them? But the days will come, when the bridegroom shall be taken away from them, and then shall they fast in those days.*

He says, do you make people who are celebrating to fast? Is that the time or place for it?

Each of us may be called to fast, in our own time and need by the Spirit. But that's not something to judge another by, if your time is now and theirs isn't. You aren't better than they are, or more righteous or spiritual because you've given yourself to fast. And if you're doing it in the correct spirit, you'd know it.

But further, Jesus is saying His time is short. That He will be gone from their presence and they will have time appointed to them for fasting then.

Not content with that upbraiding of these hypocrites, He continues with another parable. Parables are common examples that may be understood on their own, to better illustrate a more difficult concept.

Jesus says, if you have an old garment to mend, you don't sew a new cloth to patch it. Because the new cloth will shrink, it will pull the stitching ripping it worse than it was. That the new isn't in agreement with the old. It doesn't match. It will wear differently.

And in a like manner, newly squeezed juice isn't put into old wine bottles. (Bottles being leather casks, designed to be water-tight to store liquids). Wine in the Bible means all juices, fresh or fermented, and I won't get into that but the drunkards seethe at this when it is pointed out. And new wine, fresh juice, of put into an old, dried out and worn cask, an old bottle, as it begins to ferment will give off gasses, expanding inside the bottle, causing it to be ruined and the wine to spill out. (While they had ways to preserve juice to prevent fermentation into alcohol, for longer term storage, most was pressed and bottled to be consumed before it could naturally occur).

These two examples of things common to that day, before modern mass consumerism gave us plastic bottles and eliminated the need to patch clothing, were things people could understand. And Jesus used it to make a point to the Pharisees who were touting their own righteousness.

They are the torn and ratty clothes. They are the warn and old bottles. What Jesus was bringing was new. A new and better testament. A new and better covenant. He wasn't there to fix the tear they'd made in their disobedience. He was going to replace it.

He wasn't there to refill their old, dried and cracked bottles, but to give new wine in bottles fit to hold it.

He says "*No man also having drunk old wine straightway desireth new: for he saith, The old is better*." He is calling them out and saying why they cannot understand Him or His preaching, or the behavior of those who desired this new thing.

He's saying no wonder you don't get it. They are drunk on old wine. They can't understand the new thing He is replacing the old with.

It is this same point we just studied in **Hebrews 8**;

*But now hath he obtained a more excellent ministry, by how much also he is the mediator of a better covenant, which was established upon better promises. For if that first covenant had been faultless, then should no place have been sought for the second. For finding fault with them, he saith, Behold, the days come, saith the Lord, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah: Not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers in the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt; because they continued not in my covenant, and I regarded them not, saith the Lord.*

 This is the "replacement theology" that Zionists deny.

Jesus is proclaiming **a more excellent ministry,** the mediator of **a better covenant,** which was established upon **better promises.**

It doesn't say *Except for the Jews. Hebrews is literally written to them.

It doesn't say the Old Testament and New are coequal. The old covenant was glorious, but the fault was in the people to keep it. And so God regards them not. But in Christ, a new testament, a better covenant with better promises, one that has no fault because it doesn't require our perfection, only His.

And those still caught up in the old ways, thinking their righteousness before man was the same as righteousness before God, they refused to see it and took no heed to the parables of Jesus.
