Luke chapter 12 is almost entirely red-lettered preaching of Jesus Christ, both to the apostles and the people gathered in the assembly with them, and ultimately, a message to us, straight from the Word of God.

Jesus is before a crowd, a multitude so great people are stepping over each other to move. But we see Jesus turning to His company of disciples to say, "*Beware the leaven of the Pharisees*," to beware being hypocrites. That the sin that consumes the Jewish religious leaders is their holier than thou act, while they themselves are in sin. Casting judgment down on others while they themselves are guilty of the same and worse.

Many Christians today fall into this trap, and find themselves exposed and revealed. Nothing hidden remains hidden. Jesus says that what we whisper in secret will be proclaimed from the rooftops. Our sin is exposed when it is hidden, especially when we cover it by acting superior to others.

We are all sinners and have fallen short. So fear God, not man. Be true. Not hypocrites. God chasteness every child, scourging every son.

He tells them further, edifying them, not to fear men for the preaching of the word. Don't deny Christ because of threat and violence. God values His children. He knows us and loves us. Jesus is our advocate and brother.

Here Jesus gives the teaching of the unpardonable sin; blasphemy of the Holy Ghost. Those that mock the power by which the Apostles act, the Holy Spirit which seals us as God's. The person of the Godhead which rebukes the world for its sin. Reprobates hate this pricking of their hearts, and the revealed judgment of God by the Holy Spirit, and it is that judgment that causes them to despise the truth that they may have their conscience seared, to do those things that are not convenient. To be given over and given up by God. To be rejected. Made reprobate.

He gives advice to them that will be delivered up to the authorities by the Jews, that the Holy Ghost brings to them what to say. Don't plan arguments and speeches. God will bring to remembrance scripture, and give a measure of wisdom in peril through the Holy Ghost.

Jesus is giving all this advice, straight doctrine, and is interrupted by a man with a petty dispute, seeking his brother to share an inheritance. Greedy and covetous, asking Christ Jesus, the son of God in the midst of preaching fire, to judge this trifling matter of earthly treasure.

He gives the parable of the rich man who stored his excess wealth up on earth, while neglecting what matters, spiritual things, treasure for God. So that having stored this wealth and bounty in covetousness, God takes his life, leaving all of it to rust, rot and moth. Worthless to the man before the judgment of God.

*The life is more than meat, the body more than raiment.* We should not care so much about these things, God will provide. Seek to store up treasure in Heaven and we will have what we need here on earth.

He says, you can't think yourself taller, you can't change your height by worry, that's under God's control, so why worry about the rest? Trust Him. Have faith. Seek the kingdom of God.

God wants to provide for us. Not wealth and riches and material things, these may come, we may have seasons of plenty, we might be poor, but learn to be content regardless as all comes from God, and we know this having the treasure of eternal life and a part in the Kingdom of God. Value that more than things or comfort.

*For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.*

And by doing this, by waiting patiently doing the work of the Lord, diligently seeking His will and loving others, to do that which we who are anointed by the Spirit are called to do; preach the Gospel to the poor, heal the broken hearted, give comfort and liberty to those in bonds, when the Lord comes we will not be taken unawares. We will discern the times. We will be ready for the feast.

Peter asks if Jesus just means the apostles or is this advice, touching on end times prophecy, for everyone that believes. Jesus says simply blessed is the servant who when the Lord comes He finds so doing. It's for all of us. And by doing His will, by being loyal and watchful servants, by storing up treasure in heaven, we will be rewarded  as rulers with Him in the kingdom.

Jesus then warns about becoming impatient and in doing so, slipping into the way of the Pharisees, the leaven of hypocrisy. Being slack. Worried about the things of this world. Feasting. Drunk. Mistreating others. He warns that such a person who in His name, who knows His will but does it not, they will be severely treated, beaten with many stripes. Even worse than the unbelieving, who act in ignorance.

Jesus preaches the truth that to believe in Him brings division, that the faith will divide even families. It's how it is, be prepared and know the signs.

Behave as if you're being taken to judgment by an adversary, being honest in your dealings that you're blameless before the magistrate and not cast into prison, for if you're not, you'll be given no mercy. You'll pay every cent you are found to owe.

His warnings and edifying, to be good and faithful servants, to fear only God, to serve those we are called to, to act right, judge properly, placing your heart on the Kingdom not the cares of this world, given to inspire us in our walk with Him, are important to keep in mind, babe in Christ, or, and especially, as a more mature Christian. Not to lose sight of the prize. In patience and longsuffering we wait and do, that we may be blessed at the returning of the Lord.

I feel weird about trying to give a study of what Jesus is saying here, when His words are so plain and easily understood, His parables in this passage aren't dark sayings, He is desperately trying to impart these things to His disciples before His eventual crucifixion. It's a ticking clock we see Jesus is all too aware of.

*But I have a baptism to be baptized with; and how am I straitened till it be accomplished!*

Straitened, meaning constrained to a narrow path, Jesus laments showing frustration at this hypocritical generation. That they don't see it all clearly, and the press of time is all too real for Him that was before time, now made in corruptible flesh that He may deliver man.

Some people say things like "we need to just focus on the red letters, and not worry so much about other doctrines and disputes over scripture!" But that's a natural man misunderstanding; the red letters ARE the scriptures, Jesus is the Word of God. His preaching and parables are the fulfilment of the law, the doctrines of God. They aren't isolated or contradictions. I mention this because, in my experience, people who say that don't actually read the red letters. It's a cope to not have to deal with the meaning and implications of the Bible. To really study the word and understand the fundamentalism Jesus is preaching.

By the same token, we can be lost in the weeds of doctrine at times. It is a good thing to really consider the words of Jesus, and apply them to our lives. Praying on them that we can see the revealed will of God.

Jesus lived in the flesh a short while, His earthly ministry only 3 and a half years, the Gospels our only record of His teachings, teachings He knew He had so little time to convey. Go back and really read and consider the chapter, in that light. Spend time with the words of Jesus, it will change you. Amen

It is important to point out that in chapter 13 of Luke, which I covered somewhat this morning, much of the preaching done by Jesus, if not all of it, was not to disciples, to the saved, though many may have been present and there is application for us today as believers. It was to non-believers and, especially as His ministry wound down to His eventual crucifixion, He is preaching harder and harder against the reprobate Jews. The holy men, so called, hypocrites and vipers. And those they've made twice the child of Hell as themselves.

They are the fowls of the air, perching on the mustard tree that is the Kingdom of Heaven. They are the leaven hidden in the meal that spreads throughout. They are those who seek to enter by the wide gate of their works and self-righteousness. They are those without the white raiment given the guests of the wedding who came when bidden, crashing the wedding.

They are those saying "Lord, Lord, look upon my works." The virgins without oil in their lamps. The servant who didn't think the Lord would come, and instead ate, drank and was merry. They are the man counted among the share of the unbelieving. The man, given much who received the worse stripes.

They, knowing the judgment of God reject it. They put off getting right with God, obeying the Gospel, thinking that when brought before the magistrate they will be able to plea their case.

They are those who rather than striving towards the strait gate, contending for the faith, that they may be saved to do the work of the Lord, count on their genealogies and self-righteous works and adhering to the letter of the law, the ordinances and customs, but inside are whited sepulchers. Full of dead men's bones. Faithless and hopeless. Tares among the wheat, fit to be gathered and burned. The tree without fruit. Unable to come to repentance. Reprobate silver.

It's important to understand that the Bible is deep, and it is complex, and when scripture is telling us God's word, when Jesus speaks it is to all men. Saved men. Unsaved men. Reprobates.

There are lessons for us all, and deep with doctrine. But understand Jesus preaches hard against those too blind to see, dull of hearing, hearts hardened, as much as He speaks to His disciples, and for the same reason; to get those willing to listen to reconsider and obey the Gospel of reconciliation and grace.

Continuing a theme from **Luke 12** that I touched on [last night](https://t.me/HouseOfWews2/9465), where Jesus is preaching the Kingdom of Heaven, and specifically addressing those who would not believe, mostly among the Pharisees, as a way of contrast that the other people may see the chief among them's error, and come to repent towards God.

Here, He has gone to supper bidden by a Pharisee, and sat among them on a sabbath, the Bible says, that they watched Him. Observing Jesus, looking to tempt Him as they've been. Looking to find fault. Some undoubtedly seeking status on f having supper with Him, as His ministry had grown. Looking for shared glory by proximity.

It reminds us of Jesus having said in chapter 12: *Lord, Lord, open unto us; and he shall answer and say unto you, I know you not whence ye are: Then shall ye begin to say, We have eaten and drunk in thy presence, and thou hast taught in our streets. But he shall say, I tell you, I know you not whence ye are; depart from me, all ye workers of iniquity.*

And here we see them eating with Christ, just as He said.

The point is in the judgment, being in proximity to Christ isn't the same as believing on Christ. Doing works in His name, eating supper, His work done in your streets, in your church or even calling Him Lord, isn't sufficient to be saved.

To receive the imputed righteousness of Jesus. To be washed clean in His blood. That comes by faith alone, coming to understand that you are a sinner deserving death and Hell, and accepting the free gift of grace, forgiveness and reconciliation.

In the parable of the 10 virgins, waiting for the bridegroom that they may attend his wedding feast, Jesus says that some had oil prepared in their lamps, and when he arrived, went out and were taken into the feast. The rest, having no oil themselves asked for some of the other's, but they could not share. You can't be saved by being the son or daughter of a saved Christian. You cannot be made righteous by being the spouse of a believer. You can't be saved by going to a Christian church, partaking in the Lord's supper, or by trying to show up at the wedding feast in your own attire, clothes in the filthy rags of your own righteousness.

That's what all these parables about weddings and being cast out into outer darkness, with wailing and gnashing of teeth, it's what all these are teaching.

After healing a man with edema, there among the Pharisees on the sabbath, Jesus again puts the hypocritical men on the spot. They seek to hold the letter of the law against Him, while the spirit of it is revealed in the exceptions given to help a neighbor or even an enemy.

Then He gives those bidden to the supper like He was some advice in humility and how the wisdom of men differs from that of God.

Jesus says, if you're invited to a party, don't go in assuming you're asked to sit in the high places of status, instead be seated in the lowest room. Just happy to be there, and so when the lord of the supper bids you to sit in a more privileged seat, you are truly honored. If you presume, and you're asked to give up your spot to one greater than you, you will be humiliated. It's a basic teaching on how life works, and how it is in the Kingdom, that these social climbers and clout seeking Pharisees miss.

Jesus goes on to say; *when thou makest a feast, call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind: And thou shalt be blessed; for they cannot recompense thee: for thou shalt be recompensed at the resurrection of the just.*

If you have the means to call a feast, humbly seek to serve those who cannot do anything for you. Who are week. Honor them without thought for reward in this life and be rewarded for it at the judgment. It is the counterpoint advice for hosts, paired with how guests should behave.

This pattern holds true in the Kingdom to come.

He then gives the parable of the wedding feast, where the honored guests all refuse the invitation with their excuses, the cares of the world. Those bidden refuse to come. He is speaking to the Pharisees, saying they are like them.

The feast will go on. The Lord will invite those poor and lame and of no status, that his house be filled. He will send his servants to the highways and hedges and compel the meek and lowly, bidding them to the feast. Those originally bidden, the Jews, the hypocritical religious leaders, they won't taste of this supper.

Another message Jesus began mentioning increasingly as His time drew near, was that of discipleship. Of not just salvation by faith, and the fulfilment of the promise made of God for a Christ, but that of those who would pick up their cross and follow Him. Those who would, for love of Him, forsake everything to serve Him, and what that would mean.

He called Peter, Andrew, James and John to be fishers of men, to forsake family and the family's business as fishermen, and they left all. Due to Jesus' intervention, they filled their nets so much so the boats began to capsize. They had the richest catch of their lives, and left it behind on the beaches of Galilee for others, in order to become disciples of Christ.

This wasn't for everyone who believed. And it certainly divided off those who were there only for the spectacle; the signs and wonders, the miracles performed, the fiery sermons preached, the dead brought back to life and demons cast out.

Jesus frequently warns there's a cost for following Him. His hard sayings brought division, and offended many that they no longer followed. His telling them that they'd be persecuted, brought before magistrates and beaten in synagogues for His name's sake, that they would see prison, and possible death for preaching the Gospel.

Jesus told those who were faithful to follow Him and be His disciples that they should go out, among the highways and hedges, with nothing but the clothes on their back and the sandals on their feet, and want for nothing, to live on faith that God would provide. To leave their family, friends, the towns they knew, the sins they were comfortable in, the ways of their former life, that they may seek rewards in Heaven, afar off, ministering to the the poor in spirit, that they may come to know the truth of God. To do more than simply believe and be saved. To do more than be in the Kingdom of Heaven, but to help reign over it. To be willing to live for Christ and not themselves.

This wasn't for everyone. Many in the crowds who believed fell away. Like the seed that falls on rocky soil that grows up with shallow roots and fades away in the heat of the sun.

Some, in the joy of their salvation and the hope they were filled with tarried longer, seeking to do some service for Christ, only to fade by and by, consumed by the cares of this world.

Many are called but few chosen. The harvest is ripe but the laborers few. The spirit willing, but the flesh weak.

It is in this context that we see Jesus, on the road to Jerusalem and the looming weight of the cross already heavy on His shoulder, and He turns to the masses that are behind Him, some saved. Some already having given up much to follow Him. Some who believed unto salvation and others unsure. And gadflies and haters of God, seeking that He fall in some way that they could accuse Him. These same sort of mixed multitudes that had been with Him throughout His ministry.

And it is in this context that He speaks to them, recorded here in Luke chapter 14.

Jesus says essentially, if anyone comes to Him, to be His disciples, and hates not his family, not only his father and mother and wife, but his brothers and sisters and his own children, and more than that, his own life, he cannot be His disciple.

Understanding that Jesus doesn't mean that we should hate them, or ourselves, but that we be willing to give them up and more, our very lives because we love Him all the more. That if the choice was given between them and Him, a disciple would choose Christ.

He says of you're not earnestly expecting to bear your cross, the implement of death used by the Romans, the equivalent to this first century group of people, pre-crucifixion, pre-resurrection, to saying a firing squad, an electric chair, lethal injection. If you're not willing to be hung from a tree in public, a gazingstock in death for those passersby, a horrific sight they may have seen themselves as it was common, Jesus says, if they would follow Him they must be prepared to face.

Jesus turns to this mass of people and says, sit down first and count the cost. Consider the price. For if they begin their discipleship and fall away in due time, they will be mocked. Ridiculed. Their faith doubted. The cause of Christ given a bad report, but more, they themselves would be seen as foolish. Taken by a trend, their service just a fad. That they didn't mean all they said.

Like a king, knowing he faces overwhelming odds, would sue for peace having scouted and reckoned the cost of war, Jesus is begging they likewise consider if they can follow after Him.

Jesus says; *Salt is good: but if the salt have lost his savour wherewith shall it be seasoned with?* You may be useful to the Lord. You may, with the best of intentions and the fullest of desire seek to be a minister, serving Him. This is good. But what if in time you lost that usefulness? Salt without savour is not only not useful, but it can't be dumped on the land for nothing there would grow, not even the dunghill, because it would ruin a compost pile. It has to be cast out.

This passage can be a downer. Jesus gets real, and many people misunderstand what's being said. Many mistakenly think this passage and others like it are about salvation, not discipleship. This error cuts two ways.

Some believe that He is describing a works-based salvation, that the works of discipleship are a way to earn righteousness and sanctification, and by this false belief fail to achieve either.

But even more common mistake, including among saved Christians, is that Jesus is describing the saved, just as they are. That by belief unto redemption that they have picked up that cross. That by nature of their being given eternal life by God's grace they have forsaken the world. That discipleship comes naturally with being born again, and they have nothing left to do but maybe go to church once in awhile and read some scripture-poasts on Telegram here and there. (Or arguing with heretics online). These passages become meaningless self-congratulatory "inspirational quotes." That when they give up some sin or another, they've picked up their cross.

It is deeper than that, and far more serious a matter to be willing to forsake everything for Christ. To be His disciples. And we should count the cost, soberly and with great care.

This isn't an admonition, I am in no position to judge, I am really only coming to count the true cost of this myself, after many many years of being saved. It is a place that some never come to, or try in youthful exuberance only to fail, but later, in maturity successfully achieve. Jesus wasn't trying to discourage us from being His disciples, but dividing the chaff from the wheat, being honest with those of us who remain.

Every born again believer is called to be in service to Christ. It is time to consider the cost.

*5 And when he hath found it, he layeth it on his shoulders, rejoicing.*

*6 And when he cometh home, he calleth together his friends and neighbours, saying unto them, Rejoice with me; for I have found my sheep which was lost.*

*7 I say unto you, that likewise joy shall be in heaven over one sinner that repenteth, more than over ninety and nine just persons, which need no repentance.*

*8 Either what woman having ten pieces of silver, if she lose one piece, doth not light a candle, and sweep the house, and seek diligently till she find it?*

*9 And when she hath found it, she calleth her friends and her neighbours together, saying, Rejoice with me; for I have found the piece which I had lost.*

*10 Likewise, I say unto you, there is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner that repenteth.*

*13 And not many days after the younger son gathered all together, and took his journey into a far country, and there wasted his substance with riotous living.*

*14 And when he had spent all, there arose a mighty famine in that land; and he began to be in want.*

*15 And he went and joined himself to a citizen of that country; and he sent him into his fields to feed swine.*

*16 And he would fain have filled his belly with the husks that the swine did eat: and no man gave unto him.*

*17 And when he came to himself, he said, How many hired servants of my father's have bread enough and to spare, and I perish with hunger!*

*18 I will arise and go to my father, and will say unto him, Father, I have sinned against heaven, and before thee,*

*20 And he arose, and came to his father. But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him.*

*21 And the son said unto him, Father, I have sinned against heaven, and in thy sight, and am no more worthy to be called thy son.*

*22 But the father said to his servants, Bring forth the best robe, and put it on him; and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet:*

*23 And bring hither the fatted calf, and kill it; and let us eat, and be merry:*

*24 For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found. And they began to be merry.*

*25 Now his elder son was in the field: and as he came and drew nigh to the house, he heard musick and dancing.*

*26 And he called one of the servants, and asked what these things meant.*

*27 And he said unto him, Thy brother is come; and thy father hath killed the fatted calf, because he hath received him safe and sound.*

*28 And he was angry, and would not go in: therefore came his father out, and intreated him.*

*29 And he answering said to his father, Lo, these many years do I serve thee, neither transgressed I at any time thy commandment: and yet thou never gavest me a kid, that I might make merry with my friends:*

*30 But as soon as this thy son was come, which hath devoured thy living with harlots, thou hast killed for him the fatted calf.*

*31 And he said unto him, Son, thou art ever with me, and all that I have is thine.*

*32 It was meet that we should make merry, and be glad: for this thy brother was dead, and is alive again; and was lost, and is found.*

Here in Luke chapter 15 we see that again, the Pharisees and scribes murmured amongst themselves, judging Jesus for the publicans and sinners that were drawn to hear His preaching. And again, Jesus shows them in parable that He is come to bring the lost sheep home. He has come to bring sinners to repentance towards God, not the righteous. A physician treats the sick.

And Jesus tells how much joy there is in Heaven when one sinner turns towards God that they may be saved. He offered the example of the lost sheep, and another of a lost piece of silver, and the rejoicing of those who had found what was lost, comparing that to God the Father and His angels rejoicing over every saved believer, even the most wicked and wretched.

To drive the point home, Jesus tells what has become one of the most iconic parables in scripture. The Prodigal Son. This story of falling and forgiveness, the love of a father for a son thought lost to the world, and the joy at his being restored home is well known even outside of Christian circles. It is an archetype used in secular stories, referred to throughout the culture, and the phrase "prodigal son" part of our lexicon.

The tearful joy of the Father at having his son returned to him, all that he'd done forgiven in an instant, has been a moving inspiration to millions seeking redemption in Christ. The lesson that no matter how far we fall, we are still welcome home by God, Who celebrates our return with joy has helped heal so many similarly lost, and brought them home through Christ.

It has moved me to tears to read it over the years. First as a sinner, come to God saying "Father, I have sinned against heaven, and before you, And am not worthy." But especially as a father of grown children, being able to relate to that kind of heartache and love. The shift in my life's perspective, changing the meaning and adding depth to my appreciation of Jesus' words.

But that's not who the parable is addressed to here. It's not addressed to the repentant sinner. It's not addressed to God the Father, for certain. It's addressed to those Pharisees and scribes, ostensibly righteous men, who are casting judgment on the sinners who're called by faith to Christ.

They are the elder son. The son, who by nature didn't rebel and stayed, doing the work on the farm for the father, who was there while his brother went after whoredoms and drunkenness. Who stayed true. And who, feeling entitled by his works came to anger at his father, resenting his brother and refusing to celebrate his return.

How many saved Christians today are like the elder son? Many who grew up in Christian homes, given the advantage of hearing the Gospel regularly, attending church where the Bible was preached, seeing the testimony of their own family, their parents, friends and congregants living out their Christian walk before them, and who, seeing new converts coming into the church, babes in Christ saved from a life of indulgence and sin, often scarred and broken, traumatized by the damage done in their lives and seeking to be healed, and came to resent them? To be holier than thou? Hypocrites? Fruit inspectors?

It's happened. It was the case of the Pharisees, many of whom were not saved by faith but being so immersed in the culture of the religion believed they were righteous by their own works and in a place to judge others. The beam in their eye blinding them.

Even those long-saved, but grown prideful, forgetting their previous state and losing sight of the mercy God showed them, the grace given to their undeserved salvation. Thinking they are better than.

These are often those who seek to add works to the gospel of grace. Who push Lordship and outward signs of turning from sin before things like longsuffering, charity, instruction. Who have the leaven of the Pharisees in their hearts, which is hypocrisy.

These types drive wedges between brothers, sow discord in the assembly, and have torn down entire church families, turning off an unknown multitude from receiving the Gospel by their bad report. Placing stumbling blocks before others, reminding them of their old man constantly.

The Bible says *As far as the east is from the west, So far hath he removed our transgressions from us.* God says, *their sins and iniquities will I remember no more.*

As Jesus puts it, *Likewise, I say unto you, there is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner that repenteth.*

This must be our attitude as Christians towards others. To love with the charitable love Jesus gave us. Longsuffering. Merciful. With grace. Forgetting about the past. Not holding grudges. Being understanding of the frailties of others, knowing with humility exactly how frail we are ourselves.

This is not to say we ignore sin, or compromise what is right. There is church discipline for a reason, and it is outlined by Jesus and the epistles for our use. Right is right. If God says it's a sin, we ought have no other opinion on the matter. We teach and preach separation. Feeding the new man that the old man may fade away. Edifying one another. Steel sharpening steel.

But we correct in love. We deal with the beam in our eye so that we may help others with the mote that is in theirs. We forgive when sincere apology is made. We forget, so that there is no resentment or grudge. We avoid the leaven of hypocrisy. We celebrate the return of the lost, rejoicing in their salvation.

*It was meet that we should make merry, and be glad: for this thy brother was dead, and is alive again; and was lost, and is found.*

Amen

**Luke 16**
*And he said also unto his disciples, There was a certain rich man, which had a steward; and the same was accused unto him that he had wasted his goods.*

*3 Then the steward said within himself, What shall I do? for my lord taketh away from me the stewardship: I cannot dig; to beg I am ashamed.*

*4 I am resolved what to do, that, when I am put out of the stewardship, they may receive me into their houses.*

*5 So he called every one of his lord's debtors unto him, and said unto the first, How much owest thou unto my lord?*

*6 And he said, An hundred measures of oil. And he said unto him, Take thy bill, and sit down quickly, and write fifty.*

*7 Then said he to another, And how much owest thou? And he said, An hundred measures of wheat. And he said unto him, Take thy bill, and write fourscore.*

*8 And the lord commended the unjust steward, because he had done wisely: for the children of this world are in their generation wiser than the children of light.*

*9 And I say unto you, Make to yourselves friends of the mammon of unrighteousness; that, when ye fail, they may receive you into everlasting habitations.*

*10 He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much: and he that is unjust in the least is unjust also in much.*

*11 If therefore ye have not been faithful in the unrighteous mammon, who will commit to your trust the true riches?*

*12 And if ye have not been faithful in that which is another man's, who shall give you that which is your own?*

*13 No servant can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon.*

We are in **Luke 16.** The chapter opens with Jesus speaking to His disciples, again impressing upon them the lessons He must as He makes His way to Jerusalem. Here, Jesus tells them parable of the unfaithful steward.

A dishonest steward is to be fired by his wealthy master for mismanagement of the lord's funds. Knowing he'd be out of a job, and not suited to labor or begging, decides to use his position to make deals with his master's debtors, forgiving their debts that they give him favor when he needs it. Buying their loyalty so when he's fired he can go to them for help. The master sees this scheme and, being corrupt himself can't help but be impressed by the servant's wisdom, his chutzpah and cunning.

And the lesson here for His disciples isn't that these men are good, or saved, but that sometimes the unsaved, in serving Mammon, understand better how the world works. How to win friends and influence people. *For the children of this world are in their generation wiser than the children of light.*

And so, Jesus says make friends with your wealth. Spend it to others benefit. Forgive them debts. Gain favor the way the unscrupulous servant has, that those you've helped may hear the Gospel, having had the trust gained, and welcome them in the Kingdom one day.

*He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful in much: and he that is unjust in the least is unjust also in much.*

Your wealth does you no good here. Being stingy, miserly, storing up wealth in this world, is forsaking wealth in the next. In parallel passages the Bible says store up our wealth in heaven.

If a worldly unsaved man understands that he can use his position and wealth, the forgiveness of debts to gain favor with men against his future calamity,  how can a saved man not see it? There's more important things than money. Think of that future and how what you have can gain against our future in Heaven.

So, if we are greedy and niggardly, unwilling to give all charitably that we may do the work of Christ, how can God trust us with actual treasure? Incorruptible crowns? Authority in the Kingdom.

If we can't be just with unrighteous Mammon, how will we expect to be just with others souls?

*Ye cannot serve God and Mammon*.

This is a theme Jesus has been hammering home; the cost of discipleship.

Jesus said we must be willing to hate our family for His sake, and willing to give up our lives. To love others more than ourselves. To not worry for earthly things like food, shelter, raiment. To be willing to forsake all in service to others, that the Gospel be shared.

And, to use what wealth we have in that same service to Christ. *Lay not up ye treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal: but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal: for where your treasure is, there will your heart be.*

Of all the warnings of the costs of true discipleship, of truly following Christ, this one against Mammon, love of money, not only giving up trying to be rich and gaining stuff, but giving away the stuff you already have, is the hardest for most people to face.

There is no "prosperity gospel." God provides what we need and knows our needs even when we don't. We may even be blessed with wealth but it's not our own. We are supposed to give all, and yet most of us don't even want to give a 10% tithe to our own church.

This can be greed, and it often is. Jealously guarding our treasure here. That it's where our heart is, not Heaven.

But for many, it's fear. Fear of doing without. Fear that God won't take care of us. That if we give away that which is extra in our lives that others benefit and by our works, God be glorified, we will suffer need. This fear grips especially tight in times like this where the debt economy, inflation and taxation and other worldly pressures weigh heavily upon us.

We may not be called to forsake everything we own. But we are called to at least consider it and do it where appropriate, in the measure called for. To be hospitable. Charitable. To do unto others without thought of ourselves and our own comfort.

In two more chapters we will see the rich young man sit down with Jesus and say in all things he is righteous before the law, and Jesus will say ok, sell everything you have and give it all away to follow Me. And the rich young man will walk away. He was being shown the error of his thinking that he was righteous by his works, and most of us won't be called to forsake all. God knows our limitations and infirmities. But we are called to give. To be as wise as this worldly unsaved steward. To not serve Mammon while claiming to serve God.

The emphasis on discipleship that Jesus keeps preaching, the cost and expectations that he has for us to truly be called followers of Christ, not just saved from hell but laying up treasures in Heaven, should have us all feeling convicted. That we're not doing enough.

Most saved Christians will tell you that they would gladly lay down their life for the cause of Christ. That rather than deny Him, we would suffer death in His name. Knowing we have eternal life and knowing that it was a gift, we would gladly lay it down. Out of love and gratitude for the grace that was shown us.

And we may sincerely mean it, although it's easy to say, knowing that it's unlikely to ever come up. It's a cheap hyperbolic brag. Our lives are not our own and having the comfort of the blessed hope of eternal life means that threats of death are threats with Heaven. But even so we know it likely will never be asked of us and so it's easy to say.

But how many saved Christians are willing to lay down 15-20 minutes of our morning to read the Bible? How many saved Christians are willing to go to church once a week, let alone three times a week? To go door knocking and soul winning? To give what extra they have in wealth and in time to the service of others that God may be glorified in us?

How can we expect to seriously be willing to go to our death for professing the name of Christ if we won't be inconvenienced a little bit here and there?

I speak this to my own shame.

And understand there are unsaved people, people working their way to heaven with the false gospel of works, who do more to help those in need than actually saved Christians today.

 I'll tell you truthfully there are reprobates who for wicked reasons give of their time and their money, that benefit the poor and the needy, more than some saved Christians are willing to do.

Count the cost of discipleship. Understand that Christianity isn't just an identity, a scene, a cheap ideological category to cosplay as, the way political and cultural identities are used today. It is not a set of arguments that we have prepackaged for us to spout off against others who have absorbed and regurgitated the ones they've consumed.

Way too many of us who claim to be saved treat it that way. I say this out of love. I say this to chastise myself as much as to motivate you.

When I count the cost, and reckoning my efforts, I find I do the bare minimum for Christ, and sometimes less than that. If you're honest with yourself, you'll find the same.

There are people like this unfaithful servant who do favors for others that they may gain in this life, and in doing so bless other people more than saved Christians who profess the Gospel and have the spirit within them. Strive to do more.

*He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much: and he that is unjust in the least is unjust also in much. If therefore ye have not been faithful in the unrighteous mammon, who will commit to your trust the true riches?*

This is a hard saying. This is difficult to hear. We are so caught up in touting our own righteousness that we missed the point of having it entirely.

Jesus isn't Joel Osteen. He doesn't preach a gospel of comfort and wealth.

If we seek to grow in our Christian life, we need to recognize the cost asked of us for following Him. And that starts with daily Bible reading and prayer.

And the more we read the Bible, the more we understand what is expected of us. With more knowledge comes more expectation. To whom much is given much is required.

The more you know, the more you realize you're half-assing it. Some will count the cost and fall away, castaway. Like the seed that falls on unfertile ground. Few will strive for the faith and contend for the crowns incorruptible. To produce fruit a hundredfold.

We should consider this before feeling comfortable in our salvation. That we are prepared to do all for Christ.

*And the Pharisees also, who were covetous, heard all these things: and they derided him.*

We see the transition here in chapter 16 of Luke, from Jesus addressing His disciples, to the Pharisees, who hearing His preaching, derided Him. They were covetous, the Bible says.

Covering means to resent those with something we lack coupled with the desire to possess that which isn't ours to have. Covetousness, which is idolatry according to scripture, is a sin because by its very nature shows a lack of gratitude towards God, and makes us bring evil towards our neighbors. Here the Pharisees are hearing Jesus preach on serving God rather than Mammon, not taking care for the things of this world, but rather laying up treasures in Heaven, and Luke, writing in the Spirit points out their covetousness. This preaching offends them. Preaching against sin brings two reactions in those that hear; conviction and repentance towards the truth or despising the messenger and the message, and doubling down in sin.

The Pharisees derided Jesus. Insulted Him. Called Him names and mocked His teachings, that had cut them to the quick.

And Jesus says to them; *Ye are they which justify yourselves before men; but God knoweth your hearts: for that which is highly esteemed among men is abomination in the sight of God.*

He says they follow the Law, but since John the Baptist and his preaching of the Kingdom and Christ's coming, the Law is not profitable, salvation is here.

They sought to be made justified by the works they did and the outward appearances they kept up, and by appealing to the justification before men, and when the Gospel of reconciliation is preached to them, where the praise of men matters not, but the humility and faith of a contrite heart towards God saves, they derided Him. They despised the gift.

Like Jesus said to His disciples in the previous verses, the Pharisees couldn't be trusted with the things of this world, they certainly won't be trusted for the things of the world to come.

Jesus says the Law and the prophets were to bring men to salvation when the kingdom of God is preached them. That they be fruit meet for repentance. The Law as a schoolmaster, the prophets giving witness.

Jesus says it is easier for heaven and earth to pass, than one tittle of the Law to fail. This has a double meaning, that God's law is perfect and eternal, in its purpose until the kingdom is full and perfect, and the old heavens and earth are passed away. Burnt up.

But more, here, Jesus is saying how hard they cling to the letter of the law, despite their rejection of the kingdom nigh unto them, even as Heaven and earth pass away to make way for the Kingdom. It should have prepared these men to enter into it. Instead it has left them without. They are adulterous to the faith of the prophets. They missed the point of the Law they justified themselves by. They don't see the Christ before them, and missed the point that there are none righteous, no not one. All have come short of the Glory of God.

And so, Jesus tells these covetous and hypocritical "holy men" a parable, the story of Lazarus and the rich man.

We are introduced to a certain rich man. Often in Jesus preaching he uses "a certain man" to indicate someone who is a particular type of person, that we the audience would readily recognize and know. This certain man was rich, dressed in finery, and ate not just well, but sumptuously. We get the picture here, he is very rich. And by implication, someone when covetous Pharisees would see as one justified by the reckoning of man, the way they see themselves. An exaggerated version of their ideal, and in the context of their derision against His preaching on serving Mammon.

And Jesus contrasts this certain rich man with Lazarus, a poor beggar which was laid at the gate of the rich man seeking the crumbs that fell from his plate. Moreover, Lazarus was full of sores, suffering physically, humiliated by the dogs licked his open wounds. Dogs being unclean to the eyes of the Jews. A more pathetic figure couldn't be painted.

And it came to pass both died, and Lazarus went to Heaven, and the rich man to Hell.

And we are told that the rich man lifted up his eyes to heaven while in torment, and across the great gulf fixed between hell and Heaven saw Lazarus being comforted by father Abraham, and cried out for mercy. To send Lazarus with just a little water, a finger dipped, that his tongue would feel relief from the burning hellfire.

Where in life, Lazarus begged for his crumbs, the rich man is reduced to similar begging.

*But Abraham said, Son, remember that thou in thy lifetime receivedst thy good things, and likewise Lazarus evil things: but now he is comforted, and thou art tormented. And beside all this, between us and you there is a great gulf fixed: so that they which would pass from hence to you cannot; neither can they pass to us, that would come from thence.*

Daunted, and seeking place for repentance where none can be found, the rich man begs that Lazarus return to the land of the living and preach the truth of salvation to the rich man's brothers that they may be spared this fate.

*Abraham saith unto him, They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them.*

*And he said, Nay, father Abraham: but if one went unto them from the dead, they will repent.*

*And he said unto him, If they hear not Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded, though one rose from the dead.*

Jesus makes the point emphatically. They didn't come to salvation by faith, which comes by hearing the word of God. They served Mammon, like the rich man in Hell. And just as they didn't believe Moses and the prophets, they wouldn't be persuaded though a man rose from the dead.

This has a double meaning, where there is the literal example of Lazarus, raised from the dead by Jesus in Bethany, whom the Jews saw come up from the grave after 4 days, made whole by the compassion of Jesus. And of course, Jesus speaks of His own looming death and resurrection. These vipers have hardened their hearts and wouldn't believe even if they saw the son of man rise again.

I would be remiss if I didn't address some of the contentions that come from this parable.

There are some who take this teaching of Jesus and draw conclusions from it for doctrine that amount to them attempting to fit their square pegs into round holes. Who are applying the logic of men to the things of God.

There are some who deny Heaven and Hell entirely and to them they will say that this parable shouldn't be used to justify the doctrines of Heaven and Hell being real, fixed places in the cosmos. And the destination of the dead be they saved or unsaved.

They take a general rule of thumb that is true and apply it here in a way that's foolish. We shouldn't draw doctrine from parables taken literally. We aren't literally having the faith of a mustard seed. We aren't literally sowing seeds upon the ground. We aren't literally sheep, the enemy's not literally wolves. We are supposed to see that creation serves as a way of understanding God's word, which is spirit and which is life.

But what they fail to understand is that every parable that Jesus tells is of something we can understand. Of something real. Of lamps and oil and weddings and servants, of lords and stewards. Sowing seeds and harvesting the fruit. Jesus consistently uses creation as the backbone of his parables so that man can relate to what he's saying and take from it. The spiritual application that He's providing. That's no different here. God is not the author of confusion, and Jesus doesn't make things up.

So even if this is simply a parable and not an actual retelling of events, it still uses as its basis, reality. Identifiable and understandable concepts. Death and the life thereafter, or condemnation to Hell which is burning and fire.

Another mistaken doctrine that stems from this is the idea that Abraham's bosom is a place and not a body part. That prior to Jesus crucifixion there was no Heaven and Hell but waiting areas, that Lazarus went to a paradise that is part of Hell. That Jews who were saved in the Old Testament, All of the Israelite saints, that when they die they went to Abraham's bosom rather than to Heaven where Abraham awaited.

This is often paired with dispensationalist heresies. It's foolishness and the other extreme of using parables for doctrine.

We can't say for certain that the Lazarus of this story is Jesus' friend from Bethany, the brother of Mary and Martha whom Jesus loved. But it's unusual for Jesus in a parable to use the specific name rather than a certain descriptor. It's not that important that we know this detail for sure. It's the spiritual application of the parable that matters. That there are some who see the richness of life as sumptuous living and worldly success. Who serve mammon rather than God. And their ability to believe, to come to saving faith is hampered by their pride and arrogance. Their hypocrisy and covetousness. They're placing the justification before men above being justified by God.

There is a Heaven and there is a Hell and there is more to this life than the things that we store up here on earth.

Don't allow your comfort or your wealth or your respect among your peers to confuse you regarding salvation. All have fallen short and failed to uphold God's law. And don't allow the low status of some to make you see them as less than. Don't be a respecter of persons.

*And it came to pass, as he went to Jerusalem, that he passed through the midst of Samaria and Galilee.*

And there Jesus saw ten lepers, calling out to be healed. And as was custom under the law as we saw earlier in Luke, Jesus says they are healed, go show the priests and do the sacrifices that they may be proved clean.

And all but one go off. The remaining one, a Samaritan. By implication the others were Jews. (They might not be, but it seems the purpose of God to point this out.)

The healed Samaritan stays, falling before Jesus in thanks, praising God.

Jesus asks where the other 9 were, this stranger, a non-Jew, says they can't be found, that they were healed and took off. Jesus tells Him his faith has made him whole. Not only healed physically, but saved spiritually.

Now to those of us saved spiritually, by faith, calling out "Jesus, Master, have mercy on us" that in His grace we be forgiven, there is a lesson here.

Physical healing, a picture of our spiritual healing in salvation, we see Jesus tell them to go on their way. He doesn't ask they praise God or worship Him in thanksgiving. He heals them and says to go do what you're supposed to. In this case the ritual ordinances relating to the healing of a leper. In ours, the basics of the faith, showing we are clean as it were. Turn from sin, read your Bible, say your prayers, love God, love others.

Bare minimum Christianity.

Few, maybe one out of ten as is the example here, actually realize what a gift they've been given and rather than the bare minimum, seek to serve Him more, in praise and thanksgiving.

All ten were healed. All who believe are given eternal life. But it is the rare few who follow it up with this level of devotion as pictured by the Samaritan.

Luke's Gospel has been focused on the costs and consequence of discipleship. Of what following Christ actually means. That we are not only healed, justified by faith through the grace of God in Jesus name, but how we grow our faith that we may better serve Him in gratitude.

The disciples here ask Jesus to show them how to grow their faith. He says if they had the smallest amount of faith they could uproot a sycamine tree, and plant it in the sea. A sycamine is known for its incredibly deep and strong roots. It is not just some shallow rooted pine. Jesus uses extremes in examples to give us a measure of what He means.

But His answer as to how we grow our faith actually ties in and dovetails perfectly with the story of the 10 lepers.

Jesus says that when a servant is finished with his chores in the day, the master doesn't treat him as if he's accomplished something extra. He doesn't have him come and sit and feast. What Jesus is saying is the servant did what he's supposed to do. And that the right attitude having done that bare minimum, should be *We are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our duty to do.*

This is how we grow our faith. This is Jesus answer to them to this specific pointed question.

Just as the nine lepers went and did what they were told to do, what was expected of them, didn't make them remarkable. A leper healed from his incurable illness was meant to go to the priest and offer the sacrifices and perform the rituals of cleansing to prove they were healed.

I have to note it again. The order of things here, where in the leper is healed already and then they do the things required of them. (Again, understanding that this Old Testament law was put into place as a foreshadowing of what Jesus would do specifically for the purpose of these instructions in doctrine. God is great. Amen?)

Jesus says that we can grow our faith not by doing the bare minimum but realizing that doing bare minimum of what's expected of us makes us unprofitable servants. That in our realization we become as that Samaritan who, being healed, did more. Expressing his gratitude with humility.

Again, Jesus doesn't demand this of the 10 lepers when they are healed. Only that they do what they're obliged to. Just as the servant who plows the fields and then comes in and makes the meal and serves the master is doing just the bare minimum. What he's expected to do.

It is the humility and understanding the honor that we get to serve God, being unworthy and unprofitable, doing more than the bare minimum. Without expectation of praise for what is honestly the least we can do. The following of the law. Following the commandments of God. The least we can do.

And if we seek to grow our faith, realize that that is the bare minimum and strive to do more.

And so, we have to ask ourselves, are we like the one Samaritan? Followers of Christ, doing more, willing to forsake everything for the ministry of the Gospel? Growing in our faith the more we realize just how great a gift we've been given, and so loving Jesus that we devote ourselves to following Him. Picking up our cross.

Or are we like the 9? Saved, for certain. Healed of our transgressions and doing the basics, following the commandments of the law, but little else. Doing what we ought to by obligation, and little else. Unprofitable servants. Bare minimum Christians.

Or worse, are we not even holding up that weak standard? Is our faith so little that we don't even do that which is expected. Falling short of that bare minimum expectation? Caring so little about our healing that we don't stop to praise God and seek to do more for Him except the basics, and failing to do even that.

This hits hard. I fall short. But it's the lesson that is being taught, and we cannot ignore it.

If you fall short of that bare minimum, or if you do your best to do what you're obligated to, and little else, don't judge others and their Christian walk. Don't be a stumbling block or a cause of offense. *Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling*.

Contrast the blind beggar with the rich young man. Faith vs works of self-righteousness. Who was healed and rejoiced and who was turned away sorrowful.

Consider how it is you know you are going to Heaven (or why you aren't sure). The blind beggar had no doubt that Christ would heal him, taking mercy on him, a humble man of faith who called upon His name.

The rich young man who didn't recognize Jesus for who He was while sitting right there next to Him, wanted reassurance that his works had saved him, and when told they weren't enough, that it would require him to humble himself and give up everything to be perfect, he walked away in tears.

This is the contrast between salvation by faith and salvation by works. Humility and falling on the mercy of God, vs pride, boasting at your own righteous works.

*For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.*

If you are counting on your ability to follow the commands of God, to perform ordinances and rites, sacraments and ceremony in order to enter into the kingdom of Heaven, you will be left sorrowful. If you are trusting in yourself to "be good," and "not like others who are wretched sinners," you will leave sorrowful as you're cast into outer darkness. With wailing and gnashing of teeth.

If you believe on Jesus to do it all, you can rejoice, praising God, knowing His promises are true, and thus being healed, begin to follow Him.

It's that simple, and yet so hard for so many to understand.

And so, after Luke 19, where Jesus enters Jerusalem triumphantly, with the people worshiping Jesus as God and king, riding on the colt of an ass, in fulfilment of the prophecy, and ending with the chief priests and the scribes and the chief of the people seeking to destroy Jesus, we pick up immediately afterwards. Jesus is teaching in the Temple, giving the Gospel, and a delegation of the high priests, scribes and lawyers, the religious leadership of the Jews and elders of the community, their political leaders, comes to question Jesus, asking Him; by what authority does He do these things? Who does he think He is?

They saw the spectacle, they, knowing scripture understanding the significance of what He has done, allowing Himself to be declared Lord, the promised Christ, chasing out again the money changers selling sacrifice in the Temple, and teaching the good news of the Kingdom of God and salvation, in their very seat of power.

And, seeking to destroy Him, they ask Jesus; *Tell us, by what authority doest thou these things? Or who is he that gave thee this authority?*

And Jesus, knowing their intentions and knowing that though this is His final few days before His trial and death, seeks to delay their murderous plot till the timing come, and He lay down His life on the Passover. But that time is not yet come, and so Jesus answers them with a question.

Was the baptism of John from heaven or of men?

Was this new thing John, whom the people considered a prophet, recently slain by Herod, was his baptism brought of God? Or did he come up with it on his own?

The Jewish leaders were stumped. They reason with themselves that if they answer that it was of God's authority, then Jesus could ask why they didn't get baptized. Why didn't they follow him? And, if they acknowledged that John's authority came from heaven, it answers their question of where Jesus' authority comes from.

And if they deny John, the people will turn on them.

Unable to answer, Jesus says He won't answer them either. But then, in parable He gives them what they want, in a subtle way to deny them their opportunity to arrest and kill Jesus.

Jesus tells the parable of the vineyard.

A certain man, this is the LORD God, Jehovah. The Father. He plants a vineyard. As we see by scripture, this vineyard are the people of Israel, those He made covenant with, when taking them out of Egypt. And this certain man, who is God the Father, gave power to husbandmen to take care of his vineyard. These are the religious and political leaders, the same as who had come to Jesus to tempt Him.

The leaders would know exactly what Jesus was saying.

Jesus goes on and tells of how in the time to gather the harvest, the man, who is God, sent servants, who are His prophets, and those who were in charge of the vineyard, the leaders, abused them, beat them, treated these servants of the lord of the vineyard shamefully and sent them away with nothing.

Then the lord of the vineyard sends his beloved son. That they may respect him. And seeing the heir they said, let us kill him and take the inheritance for themselves. And so they did.

And Jesus, telling them their heart, that this was to be His fate as the beloved Son of God, He asks these husbandmen, left over Israel by the Lord, Jesus asks them; *What therefore shall the lord of the vineyard do unto them?*

And Jesus, answering His own question for them says; *He shall come and destroy these husbandmen, and shall give the vineyard to others.*

Shocked and angry, understanding exactly what Jesus is saying in parable, they said "God forbid."

And citing scripture, again which these so-called men of God all know, Jesus asks;

*What is this then that is written, The stone which the builders rejected, the same is become the head of the corner? Whosoever shall fall upon that stone shall be broken; but on whomsoever it shall fall, it will grind him to powder.*

And enraged, these chief priests and scribes wished to lay hands on Jesus and kill Him there, but dared not for fear of the people.

Jesus laid the blood of the prophets, *From the blood of Abel unto the blood of Zacharias,* literally from A to Z, from the first who died upholding God's word, to the last prophet slain between the altar and the temple, all this blood be upon them. Jesus said, that their generation would pay recompense. The rebellious husbandmen who neglected the vineyard and sought to overthrow their Lord. Their kind would be destroyed by God in His wrath. Woe be upon them, these vipers. These hypocrites.

The vineyard of Israel created by God to be a light unto all nations that they may repent, they who were chosen to partake in the covenant God made with them, that they would be His people and He would be their God, that at the time of harvest, the Lord would receive the increase. The fruit thereof.

But this generation of vipers, as John the Baptist proclaimed, could not being forth fruit, no men meet for repentance.

It's important to point out and interesting to consider that the same authority who ordained John's baptism, Who sent the prophets and beloved Son, Is the same authority who put these husbandmen in charge. God the Father. Jehovah LORD.

And the vineyard, being His covenant, and the fruit thereof His people, Jesus telling them that they are rebellious to the authority that they question of Christ, that they will have the vineyard, the care of that covenant, taken from them and given to others.

To which they react, "God forbid!"

This is what is called today. Replacement Theology. This idea that the vineyard has been given to others, to be overseen by other people, Who aren't the Jews. Who aren't the Levitical priesthood. Who aren't the scribes and lawyers and Pharisees and Sadducees, the elders who were unfruitful. The rebellious husbandmen, these unfruitful vine are cut off and burned.

The covenant given to another people. A New Testament.

The idea of replacement theology is found throughout the Bible. It is not some newfound doctrine, it isn't some Paulian heresy. It is the will of God the Father.

It is just. It is righteous. It has happened.

And all those who deny it, who defend these rebellious husbandmen, let them be accursed for rejecting the judgment of God and defending the murderers of Christ Jesus.

We find Jesus, now just one day from His crucifixion, very desirous to eat the passover. He mentions this desire repeatedly, telling His disciples to go and find such and such room, and prepare *where I shall eat the passover with my disciples.*

This is the first of the holy days of the year, which begins in spring in the Hebrew calendar, the first month *Adar*.
10 days in, the lamb without blemish is brought before the people, separated from the flock. On the 14th day the lamb is slain before the congregation. The blood spread with hyssop upon the wooden door posts, in remembrance of the first passover where this saved those within the home from the angel of death, given as an ordinance by God that in future generations when asked by those children, *What mean ye by this service?*  That they would explain the sacrifice, what it meant, and how God delivered the people with the blood of the lamb. That they cast out the leaven of their households, and broke and ate unleavened bread in remembrance of their flight from Egypt.

And ordinance is a memorial service, a ritual that is designed as a picture of something, to be kept as a reminder to future generations so they would understand.

*And this day shall be unto you for a memorial; and ye shall keep it a feast to the LORD throughout your generations; ye shall keep it a feast by an ordinance for ever.*

God essentially saying, "Do this in memory of Me."

Jesus, intent to have this passover supper, before His betrayal and death, brings the disciples together, and immediately turns from the traditional Passover ordinance, the ritual observance with unleavened bread, the unfermented juice of the vine and the lamb, and gives unto them a new ordinance; what we call the Lord's supper.

Jesus being the lamb to be delivered to the high priests to be slaughtered. His body broken as the unleavened bread is broken. The cup of the fruit of the vine poured out, and divided, as His blood. Blood put upon the doorways of our hearts that we be saved from death. That it passover us.

The passover observance being a picture of Christ's death. The feast of unleavened bread, the forgiveness of sin. Being brought out of Egypt and to the promised land, a picture of our deliverance to the Kingdom of God.

This, Jesus last meal before betrayal, and in it He provides a new ordinance to be done in His memory, that when future generations may ask, *What mean ye by this service?* We have a ready answer.

The cup is the new testament in Jesus' blood, which is shed for us. The bread, His body that was broken upon the cross. We do this in memory of Jesus.

Now, understanding that an ordinance in the Bible is a memorial ritual, given by God to picture the thing which we are to remember for future generations, we see the Lord's supper is a continuation of Passover, which pictured Jesus, the Christ to come and the deliverance by God's promise, given in the blood of the lamb, the unleavened bread represented the haste of their salvation from sin, and literally their being cast out of Egypt following the angel of death coming for all the first born in the land.

Jesus is that lamb, who takes away the sins of the world. The bread now, represents His body. The cup poured out, His blood.

It is the same feast, the same observation. It is a memorial and a picture of Christ.

And like passover, a yearly observation, and an ordinance done only among the people. The saved. Those with the circumcision of the heart, and among the congregation. The assembly of believers. What we call today the church. A church is a local assembly, and we see in Leviticus and in Paul's letter to the Corinthians, that both ordinances, passover and the Lord's supper, were not to be done by the unworthy, the unsaved. Paul even says that God has made those who have partaken of it who aren't saved, who didn't do it in memory of Jesus, but for unworthy reasons, that they've been made weak, and sick, and some have been killed for profaning the ordinance.

And so the Lord's supper is a yearly observance, done within the congregation of believers, using the breaking of unleavened bread and the pouring out of the unfermented juice of the vine, done in memory of Jesus.

What it is not: It is not a means of obtaining grace or salvation. It is not a "sacrament," there are not ritual requirements for salvation given in the New Testament.

It is not done with wine. The idea that the yeast of fermentation would be present when all leaven is to be cast out, is absurd. Alcohol is used as a representation of sin throughout the Bible, as is the yeast in bread. Jesus did not bless alcohol and then say it represents His blood. It's profanity bordering on blasphemy to make that claim.

It is not literal. It is generally accepted by most denominations claiming to be of Christ that the ordinances of the Old Testament were symbolic of Christ and salvation, redemption and the resurrection. No one makes the claim that the lamb offered in passover prior to the crucifixion actually became Jesus. That the blood of the lamb offered upon the doorposts transfigured into His. We all recognize ordinances are symbolic, as God says, done as a memorial.

Jesus, who as God gave us this ordinance as a new memorial, says "do this in memory of me."

The blasphemous and foolish literalist view that the bread and alcohol served by these vipers magically transforms into flesh and blood (literally by "hocus pocus" said by a so called priest) is an abomination. Christianity is not a cannibal cult.

There are some protestant sects of Catholicism that don't go that far, but still make out that it is a sacrament, not an ordinance as the Bible calls it, and that while they reject the cannibal aspect, claim that their communion brings "the real presence of Jesus" to them.

Jesus told us that wherever two or three gather in His name, He is there. Those of us saved have the Holy Spirit within us and are in constant connection to God the Father through Christ His Son. The Lord is ever-present in all things, at all times. There is nothing that can hide Him or separate Him from those who believe.

It is foolishness, and making an idol of what should be a memorial. It cheapens it at best. It becomes rote. Done weekly. Done of habit. Whereas ordinances in scripture are special. Holy. Separate. Something done solemnly and with purpose.

Not every right-believing church does it exactly the same. Some do it monthly. Some every 3 months. Many do it during the Holy Week, during their Wednesday night service. Some encourage their congregation to do it in their home, with their family.

Some believers do it with every meal as they ask the Lord Jesus to bless their food.

These different ways of keeping the ordinance while maintaining its purpose of the remembrance of Christ's crucifixion and the gift of salvation it purchased us, are incidental. It is the spirit with which it is kept that matters. Brethren of different churches who do it differently, but in the proper spirit shouldn't argue or break fellowship.

But those who cynically use it as a means of control and claiming it doles out grace, only available through their ministers, are damnable heretics.

For those asking the only other ordinance given in the New Testament, the only other ritual remembrance that we are asked to partake in as believers, Is baptism, Which represents the death, burial and resurrection of Jesus. It is an outward profession of faith by the believer. Done, in memory of what they believe on.

And like all other biblical ordinances it is done symbolically. It is not a sacrament. It is not a ritual that provides salvation. Just as communion for the Lord's supper is done in remembrance and not as a means of obtaining righteousness.

Jesus went to Gethsemane, on the mount of Olives to pray. *Saying, Father, if thou be willing, remove this cup from me: nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done.* His sweat coming off Him as if it were blood. An angel comforting Him in His hour of need.

And so now Judas approaches with the multitude of the temple guard, and went to identify Jesus by a kiss, offered in greeting. Jesus shames him in his betrayal. He shames the guards that they come for Him in the night, armed as if Jesus were a dangerous criminal.

An apostle, identified as Peter in the Gospel of John, takes his sword and strikes a servant of the High Priest, cutting off his ear. Jesus heals the man and says to Peter, *Put up thy sword into the sheath: the cup which my Father hath given me, shall I not drink it?*

*Then took they him, and led him, and brought him into the high priest's house. And Peter followed afar off.*

The passover lamb, the first born and without blemish, is brought before the High Priest to be examined. Just as Jesus, the only begotten Son, who was without sin, is brought before the High Priest. The lamb who takes away the sins of the world.

And as Jesus suffers the blows and mocking, the accusations of those that despised Him, Peter observed from a nearby fire, the dawn approaching.

And as the Lord Jesus Christ is mistreated and shamed by the Jews, Peter is asked three times by those that recognize him, if he is one of Jesus' disciples, and three times Peter in fear denies Jesus. And as the cock crowed to signal the day, Peter issues his final denial, and the Lord turned and looked upon him, and in sorrow Peter left out, weeping.

What a blow. What a terrible reality check. To be the foremost of Jesus inner circle. His closest disciple and friend. Who had faith from the beginning that Jesus was the Christ. Whose profession of that truth was the rock, the faith, that Jesus said He would build His congregation upon. And in fear and weakness, within eyeshot of Jesus, being beaten and mocked, Peter denied Him.

The greatest believer, faced with death, denies his savior. Three times.

Sometimes, it is easy to think that in the same situation we would never do that. That we would boldly proclaim that Jesus is Lord, and gladly face death for His sake. To think our faith is greater than Peter's in this moment. Thank God for never having to be tempted this way, for if Simon Peter failed this test, even with foreknowledge given by the Christ he denied, then we can be assured we wouldn't fare any better.

But the hope is in the growth of faith Peter had, that by the end he was hated and martyred for Jesus' name.

We should consider that at this point that first holy week, that Jesus was spending His first full day in Hell, carrying the sins of the whole world. Each moment of torment must have felt like a lifetime; Jesus, as the burnt offering, the Holocaust, the propitiation of our sins that we may be justified in Him. He had 2 more full days to follow.

Many Christians gladly celebrate Easter, rejoicing that He is risen. Some will consider the pain and suffering of the cross. Few want to reflect on His torment in Hell for our sins. He who knew no sin, paying the price for us.

It's something we should reflect on.

Sadly, If you're like me, You've probably already complained to yourself about some ache or some pain or some inconvenience or some disappointment or some dread for something to come later today.

We all do it. Engaging in petty and foolish complaint over what is relatively minor.

Being mindful of the suffering of Jesus for our sins, It's difficult to carry on selfishly the way we do. Getting angry at the inconvenience others give us, or the stiffness in pain we feel in our flesh, and the weakness we have in our spirit, It's difficult to not feel guilt and sorrow in much the same way. Peter felt when he denied Christ that morning.

Not to keep hammering the same point, but just considering how many people, Not even in the world but just in your immediate 50 mile radius, Will wake up this morning and stub their toe or spill their coffee, and not only complaining their heart, but use the Lord Jesus Christ's name as an expletive. As a curse. Profaning our savior over the most fleeting and minor of offenses.

*Your fathers did eat manna in the wilderness, and are dead. This is the bread which cometh down from heaven, that a man may eat thereof, and not die. *26 Ought not Christ to have suffered these things, and to enter into his glory?*

*27 And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself.*

*28 And they drew nigh unto the village, whither they went: and he made as though he would have gone further.*

*29 But they constrained him, saying, Abide with us: for it is toward evening, and the day is far spent. And he went in to tarry with them.*

*30 And it came to pass, as he sat at meat with them, he took bread, and blessed it, and brake, and gave to them.*

*31 And their eyes were opened, and they knew him; and he vanished out of their sight.*

*32 And they said one to another, Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way, and while he opened to us the scriptures?*

*33 And they rose up the same hour, and returned to Jerusalem, and found the eleven gathered together, and them that were with them,*

*34 Saying, The Lord is risen indeed, and hath appeared to Simon.*

*35 And they told what things were done in the way, and how he was known of them in breaking of bread.*

*36 And as they thus spake, Jesus himself stood in the midst of them, and saith unto them, Peace be unto you.*

*37 But they were terrified and affrighted, and supposed that they had seen a spirit.*

*38 And he said unto them, Why are ye troubled? and why do thoughts arise in your hearts?*

*39 Behold my hands and my feet, that it is I myself: handle me, and see; for a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as ye see me have.*

*40 And when he had thus spoken, he shewed them his hands and his feet.*

*41 And while they yet believed not for joy, and wondered, he said unto them, Have ye here any meat?*

*42 And they gave him a piece of a broiled fish, and of an honeycomb.*

*43 And he took it, and did eat before them.*

*44 And he said unto them, These are the words which I spake unto you, while I was yet with you, that all things must be fulfilled, which were written in the law of Moses, and in the prophets, and in the psalms, concerning me.*

*45 Then opened he their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures,*

*46 And said unto them, Thus it is written, and thus it behooved Christ to suffer, and to rise from the dead the third day:*

*47 And that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name among all nations, beginning at Jerusalem.*

*48 And ye are witnesses of these things.*

*49 And, behold, I send the promise of my Father upon you: but tarry ye in the city of Jerusalem, until ye be endued with power from on high.*

*50 And he led them out as far as to Bethany, and he lifted up his hands, and blessed them.*

*51 And it came to pass, while he blessed them, he was parted from them, and carried up into heaven.*

*52 And they worshipped him, and returned to Jerusalem with great joy:*

*53 And were continually in the temple, praising and blessing God. Amen.*

After the third day, Jesus arose, the stone rolled away, the keys to Hell and Death, His.

*9 That if thou shalt confess with thy mouth the Lord Jesus, and shalt believe in thine heart that God hath raised him from the dead, thou shalt be saved.*

*10 For with the heart man believeth unto righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.*

His life, death, burial, resurrection and ascension has purchased for all who believe on Jesus' name, the free gift of eternal life, given by God in grace, as we are yet sinners, to be washed clean in His blood. God's word made perfect.

If you haven't put your trust in this good news, and accepted that free gift, make today the day you do.

If you believe in your heart that God loved you so much, He sent His only begotten son to die for your sin and be raised again, then confess this with your mouth in prayer, calling upon Jesus' name, and be saved. Knowing that blessed assurance of eternal security, never to be lost or taken away.
